name: Sumer
known_for: Cuneiform writing, the wheel, ziggurats, the Epic of Gilgamesh
life: Most Sumerians were farmers and herders working temple and palace lands, paid in barley rations. Cities held craftsmen, merchants, scribes and priests; children of the elite trained for years in scribal schools (edubba). Homes were mud-brick houses around a courtyard.
food: Barley was the staple: baked as flat bread and, above all, brewed into thick beer drunk through straws, with temple workers paid daily rations of bread and beer. Dates, onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, fish from canals and marshes, and mutton for the wealthy filled out the diet; the Yale culinary tablets (~1750 BCE, Babylonian) preserve the oldest written recipes, mostly stews.
summary: The first civilisation with cities and writing.
government: Each Sumerian city-state (Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish, Nippur, Eridu) was independent. Early power lay with the temple, whose priests managed land, herds and storehouses; by about 2800 BCE war leaders (lugal, 'big man') became hereditary kings who built palaces beside the temples. Assemblies of elders and citizens may have advised rulers in early times. Society ranged from the royal family and priests through scribes, merchants and craftsmen to farmers, labourers on temple estates and enslaved war captives. Reforms by Urukagina of Lagash (~2350 BCE) tried to curb officials' abuses, one of the first recorded attempts at social justice.
architecture: Sumerians built almost entirely in mud brick, since stone and timber were scarce. Temples stood on raised platforms that grew into stepped ziggurats, such as the Ziggurat of Ur (~2100 BCE), with a shrine on top where the city god lived. Cities had thick walls (Uruk's were about 9 km long), narrow lanes, courtyard houses, canals, harbours and palaces. They used the arch, the vault and the dome long before the Romans, and decorated walls with cone mosaics.
technology: Sumer produced many of civilisation's foundational inventions: cuneiform writing (from ~3200 BCE, first for accounts), the potter's wheel and the wheeled cart, the seed plough, large-scale irrigation canals and dykes, bronze casting, a sexagesimal (base-60) number system that survives in our 60-minute hour and 360° circle, standard weights and measures, and early astronomy tracking lunar months. Scribal schools taught mathematics, including multiplication tables and area calculations for fields.
rise: Farming villages of the Ubaid period (~6500–3800 BCE) in the marshy south of Mesopotamia grew larger as irrigation produced surpluses. Temples organised labour and redistributed food, and trade in timber, metals and stone, absent in the alluvial plain, required administration. During the Uruk period (~4000–3100 BCE) Uruk grew into the world's first true city of 40,000 or more people, and writing was invented to manage its economy.
fall: Sumerian cities fought each other constantly over water and land. Sargon of Akkad conquered them around 2334 BCE. After a Sumerian revival under the Third Dynasty of Ur (~2112–2004 BCE), whose king Ur-Nammu wrote the oldest surviving law code, Ur fell to Elamite invaders and Amorite migrants. Centuries of irrigation had also salinised the soil: records show farmers switching from wheat to salt-tolerant barley and yields collapsing. Sumerian died out as a spoken language by about 1800 BCE but survived as a sacred and scholarly language for nearly two thousand years.
legacy: Writing, cities, schools, written law, literature (the Epic of Gilgamesh), the wheel, the 60-based time system, and the idea of a state with officials and taxes all trace back to Sumer. Babylonians, Assyrians and later the Persians and Greeks inherited its knowledge.
culture: Each city had a patron god (Inanna at Uruk, Nanna at Ur) living in the temple. Festivals such as the New Year Akitu, epic poetry, lyres from the Royal Tombs of Ur and cylinder seals show a rich culture.

name: Akkadian Empire
life: Farmers and soldiers supplied a standing army; Akkadian became the language of administration alongside Sumerian.
food: Like Sumer, Akkad lived on irrigated barley and emmer, turned into bread and beer, with dates, sesame oil, onions and fish. State workshops issued standard rations, and sheep and goats supplied wool, milk and meat for feasts.
summary: Collapsed around the 4.2-kiloyear drought.
government: Sargon created the first territorial empire, ruling diverse city-states through loyal Akkadian governors and a standing army of perhaps 5,400 men who 'ate bread daily before him'. His grandson Naram-Sin went further, declaring himself a living god and 'king of the four quarters' of the world. Akkadian, a Semitic language, became the language of government beside Sumerian.
architecture: Akkadian kings built palaces and temples in their capital Akkad, which archaeologists have never found. Their art is known from victory monuments such as the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin, showing the king climbing a mountain above his defeated enemies, and from a bronze head possibly of Sargon.
technology: The empire standardised weights and measures and the calendar across Mesopotamia, built roads and a courier system, and developed a bureaucracy that recorded taxes and trade on clay tablets. Akkadian cuneiform became the script used across the Near East for 2,000 years.
rise: Sargon, according to legend a foundling raised by a gardener who became cupbearer to the king of Kish, seized power around 2334 BCE, defeated Lugalzagesi of Uruk and conquered all of Sumer, then campaigned from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean and Anatolia. He controlled trade routes for metals, timber and stone.
fall: Revolts broke out under almost every ruler. Around 2200–2150 BCE a severe drought, the 4.2-kiloyear event, ruined harvests in northern Mesopotamia; settlements like Tell Leilan were abandoned. Gutian highlanders from the Zagros overran the weakened state, and Akkad collapsed into a period of chaos remembered in the poem 'The Curse of Akkad'.
legacy: The Akkadian Empire became the model of universal kingship for later Mesopotamian, Persian and even Roman rulers. Akkadian remained the international diplomatic language of the Bronze Age, used in letters between Egypt, the Hittites and Babylon.
culture: Sargon's daughter Enheduanna, high priestess of Ur, is the first named author in history.

name: Babylonia
known_for: Hammurabi's law code, astronomy, the Hanging Gardens (legendary)
life: Babylon was a cosmopolitan city of perhaps 200,000 under Nebuchadnezzar, with merchants, astronomer-priests and canal farmers.
food: Babylonians ate barley bread, beer, dates, lentils, onions, leeks and garlic, cooked with sesame oil; the Yale tablets record some 25 stews of lamb, pigeon and vegetables seasoned with mint and coriander. Fish and dates were cheap staples, and the Code of Hammurabi even regulated beer sellers.
summary: Babylonian astronomers tracked planets and eclipses for centuries.
government: Babylon's kings ruled with governors, judges and scribes. Hammurabi (r. ~1792–1750 BCE) united Mesopotamia and published 282 laws on a stele, covering trade, property, family, wages and crime, with punishments that depended on social class (nobles, commoners and slaves). The Neo-Babylonian kings (626–539 BCE), notably Nebuchadnezzar II, ruled a large empire through provincial governors and deportations.
architecture: Babylon became one of the largest cities in the world, with double walls, the blue glazed-brick Ishtar Gate decorated with dragons and bulls, the Processional Way, the great ziggurat Etemenanki (probably the origin of the Tower of Babel story) and Esagila, temple of Marduk. The Hanging Gardens, one of the Seven Wonders, may have been in Babylon or, as some historians argue, in Nineveh.
technology: Babylonian scholars developed advanced mathematics, including place-value notation in base 60, solutions to quadratic equations and approximations of √2 accurate to six decimal places (tablet YBC 7289). Astronomers kept nightly diaries for over 600 years and could predict lunar eclipses and planetary positions, knowledge later used by Greek and Indian astronomers. They also produced the zodiac.
rise: Babylon was a minor town until the Amorite king Hammurabi conquered rival cities such as Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari in the 18th century BCE. Its central position on the Euphrates and control of trade made it the cultural capital of Mesopotamia for over a thousand years.
fall: The first Babylonian dynasty ended when the Hittite king Mursili I sacked the city in 1595 BCE; Kassites then ruled for four centuries. After Assyrian domination, the Neo-Babylonian Empire rose under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar, but in 539 BCE Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon, reportedly without a battle, after the unpopular king Nabonidus alienated the priesthood of Marduk.
legacy: Hammurabi's law code, Babylonian astronomy, mathematics, the 7-day week linked to planets and the zodiac influenced Greece, India and the Islamic world. Babylon became a symbol of grandeur and decadence in the Bible.
culture: The Akitu festival, the Enuma Elish creation epic and records of planetary motion kept for centuries.

name: Assyria
life: A militarised society where conscripted farmers fought seasonal campaigns and conquered peoples were resettled across the empire.
food: Assyrians farmed barley and wheat in rain-watered northern Mesopotamia and kept sheep and cattle. Ashurnasirpal II's banquet stele boasts of feeding 69,574 guests with oxen, sheep, deer, fowl, fish, bread, beer and 10,000 skins of wine.
summary: Ashurbanipal's library preserved thousands of clay tablets.
government: Assyrian kings were the god Ashur's earthly representatives and led annual military campaigns. The empire was divided into provinces governed by royal appointees, with vassal kings paying tribute. Assyrians used mass deportation, moving perhaps 4.5 million people over three centuries, to break local resistance and supply labour. A network of royal roads and relay posts carried messages, letting kings track distant provinces.
architecture: Kings built grand capitals: Assur, Nimrud (Kalhu), Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad) and Nineveh. Palaces were guarded by colossal winged human-headed bulls (lamassu) and lined with carved stone reliefs of battles, sieges, hunts and tribute. Sennacherib built an aqueduct at Jerwan and gardens at Nineveh watered by canals.
technology: Assyria was the first empire to equip mass armies with iron weapons. Its engineers built siege towers, battering rams and ramps, and organised cavalry and logistics on a new scale. Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh collected about 30,000 clay tablets on medicine, omens, literature and science, preserving the Epic of Gilgamesh.
rise: Assur was a trading city whose merchants ran a famous network into Anatolia (the Kültepe tablets, ~1900 BCE). After centuries of ups and downs, the Neo-Assyrian Empire expanded from 911 BCE under kings such as Ashurnasirpal II, Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II and Sennacherib, eventually ruling from Egypt to western Iran.
fall: After Ashurbanipal's death (~631 BCE), civil war between his sons weakened the empire. Babylonians under Nabopolassar and the Medes under Cyaxares rebelled and sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; the last Assyrian army was defeated at Harran (609) and Carchemish (605). A drought may also have contributed.
legacy: Assyria created the model of the provincial empire later used by Babylon and Persia. Its reliefs are treasures of the British Museum and the Louvre, and its library preserved much of Mesopotamian literature.
culture: Lion-hunt reliefs, winged bull guardians (lamassu) and the Library of Ashurbanipal.

name: Ancient Egypt
known_for: Pyramids, hieroglyphs, mummification, the solar calendar
life: Farmers' lives followed the Nile's three seasons; during the flood they worked on royal projects for pay. Scribes, priests and artisans lived in towns; workers' villages like Deir el-Medina left letters, receipts and even records of strikes.
food: Bread and beer made from emmer and barley were so basic that wages were paid in them; onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, lettuce and Nile fish were everyday foods. The rich ate beef, roast fowl, figs, pomegranates, honey cakes and wine; tomb paintings show bakeries and breweries in detail.
summary: Lasted three millennia, ending with Cleopatra and Rome.
government: The pharaoh was a living god, son of Ra, responsible for maat, the cosmic order. Beneath him the vizier ran the government, with officials for treasury, granaries and public works, and nomarchs governing the 42 provinces (nomes). Priests controlled enormous temple estates. Scribes, trained for years, kept records of taxes, harvests and labour. Women could own property, run businesses and sue in court, more rights than in most ancient societies.
architecture: Egyptians built in stone for eternity: the Step Pyramid of Djoser (~2670 BCE, designed by Imhotep), the Great Pyramid of Giza (~2560 BCE, 146 m tall), the Sphinx, the temples of Karnak and Luxor with their forests of columns, Hatshepsut's terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari, the rock-cut tombs of the Valley of the Kings and Ramesses II's Abu Simbel. Ordinary homes were mud brick.
technology: Egypt developed hieroglyphic writing and papyrus paper, the 365-day calendar based on the Nile and the star Sirius, advanced surveying and geometry for re-marking fields after floods, medicine described in the Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri (including surgery and hundreds of remedies), mummification, glass and faience, sails and large ships, the shaduf for lifting water, and remarkable stone-cutting and transport techniques.
rise: Farmers and herders settled the Nile valley as the Sahara dried after about 5000 BCE. Chiefdoms in Upper and Lower Egypt competed until King Narmer (or Menes) united them around 3100 BCE. The Nile's predictable flood gave reliable harvests; the desert protected Egypt from invasion; and the river was a highway for trade and administration.
fall: Egypt's 3,000-year history passed through the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by 'intermediate periods' of division often linked to droughts and weak kings. After the New Kingdom collapsed around 1070 BCE, Egypt was ruled by Libyans, Nubians (Kushites), Assyrians and Persians. Alexander the Great conquered it in 332 BCE, founding the Greek Ptolemaic dynasty, which ended when Cleopatra VII died and Rome annexed Egypt in 30 BCE.
legacy: Monumental architecture, the solar calendar (adopted by Julius Caesar), medicine, mathematics, and a fascination that shaped Greek, Roman and modern culture. Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822, using the Rosetta Stone, founded Egyptology.
culture: Gods such as Ra, Osiris, Isis and Hathor; festivals like Opet; mummification and the Book of the Dead; painted tombs, music, board games (senet) and cosmetics.

name: Hittite Empire
known_for: Early iron, the first known peace treaty (Kadesh)
life: Farmers, chariot warriors and scribes in a kingdom bound by treaties with vassals.
food: Hittites ate barley and emmer bread in dozens of named shapes, porridge, lentils, figs, grapes, honey and cheese. Beer and wine were offered to gods, and royal storage pits at Hattusa could hold grain for thousands of people for a year.
summary: Fell in the Bronze Age collapse.
government: The Hittite great king ruled from Hattusa with a council of nobles (the panku), managed vassal kings by written treaties sworn before gods, and had a law code with fines rather than mutilation for many crimes.
architecture: Hattusa had 6 km of walls with the Lion Gate, the Yazılıkaya rock sanctuary with carved gods, and huge granaries.
technology: Early iron working, light three-man chariots, and archives of thousands of cuneiform tablets in several languages.
rise: Hattusili I unified central Anatolia around 1650 BCE; Mursili I sacked Babylon in 1595 BCE; Suppiluliuma I made the Hittites a superpower rivalling Egypt.
fall: Around 1180 BCE drought, famine, attacks by the Kaska and Sea Peoples and internal strife led to the abandonment of Hattusa during the Bronze Age collapse.
legacy: The Treaty of Kadesh (~1259 BCE) with Ramesses II is the oldest known peace treaty; Hittite is the oldest written Indo-European language.
culture: The 'thousand gods' of Hatti, laws milder than Babylon's, and royal archives at Hattusa.

name: Phoenicia
known_for: The alphabet, purple dye, sea trade, Carthage
life: Sailors, merchants, dyers and shipbuilders lived in crowded island and harbour cities.
food: Phoenicians ate barley and wheat bread, olives and olive oil, fish, figs and dates, and traded wine across the Mediterranean in amphorae. Their colonists spread vine and olive cultivation to North Africa and Spain.
summary: Their alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin and Arabic scripts.
government: Independent city-states such as Tyre, Sidon and Byblos were ruled by kings with powerful merchant councils.
architecture: Harbour cities with breakwaters and dry docks; Carthage's circular military harbour (cothon).
technology: The 22-letter consonantal alphabet (~1050 BCE), Tyrian purple dye made from murex snails, glass production, and navigation by the Pole Star that took them past Gibraltar and possibly around Africa (Herodotus).
rise: After the Bronze Age collapse weakened Egypt and the Hittites, the Phoenician cities filled the trade vacuum from about 1200 BCE and founded colonies across the Mediterranean.
fall: They fell under Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian domination; Alexander destroyed Tyre in 332 BCE after a seven-month siege.
legacy: Their alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic and possibly Brahmi scripts.
culture: Gods Baal and Astarte; ivory carving, glassware and the alphabet carried across the Mediterranean.

name: Ancient Israel and Judah
life: Most people farmed hill terraces growing grain, olives and grapes; life centred on clans and village elders.
food: The Seven Species of the Bible — wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates (honey) — were the basis of the diet. Most people ate bread, lentil stews, cheese and yoghurt from goats and sheep; meat was for festivals and sacrifices, and dietary laws (kashrut) defined permitted animals.
summary: Its scriptures shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
government: Early Israelites were tribes led by judges; according to the Bible, Saul, David and Solomon ruled a united monarchy (~1050–930 BCE), which split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Prophets criticised kings for injustice.
architecture: Jerusalem's First Temple (traditionally Solomon's), Hezekiah's water tunnel (~700 BCE) and fortified cities like Megiddo and Lachish.
technology: Terrace farming of hill country, water cisterns, and early Hebrew alphabetic writing.
rise: Hill-country villages emerged around 1200 BCE; the kingdoms formed around the 10th–9th centuries BCE.
fall: Assyria destroyed Israel in 722 BCE and deported its people; Babylon destroyed Judah and the Temple in 587 BCE and exiled its elite to Babylon.
legacy: The Hebrew Bible, ethical monotheism, the Sabbath and prophetic ideas of justice shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
culture: Sabbath, Passover and Temple worship; the Hebrew Bible's law, prophecy and poetry.

name: Kingdom of Kush
known_for: Nubian pyramids, ruled Egypt as the 25th dynasty, iron-working
life: Farmers along the Nile, herders and ironworkers; powerful queen mothers (kandakes) shaped politics.
food: Kushites grew sorghum, millet and barley along the Nile and kept large herds of cattle, which were symbols of wealth. They also ate fish, dates and dom palm fruit and drank sorghum beer.
summary: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt.
government: Kushite kings were chosen from the royal family with priestly approval; queen mothers and ruling queens (kandakes), such as Amanirenas who fought Rome, held great power.
architecture: Over 200 steep pyramids at Meroë and Nuri, temples at Jebel Barkal and Naqa.
technology: Meroë was a major iron-smelting centre with slag heaps still visible; Meroitic script (still only partly understood).
rise: Kush grew south of Egypt and, under Piye, conquered Egypt around 744 BCE, ruling as the 25th dynasty.
fall: Assyrians drove them out of Egypt (~656 BCE); Kush continued at Meroë until Aksum conquered it around 350 CE.
legacy: One of Africa's great early states; Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt.
culture: The lion god Apedemak, Nubian pyramids and Meroitic script.

name: Carthage
life: A merchant and maritime people with large farming estates in Tunisia.
food: Carthaginians farmed wheat, barley, olives, grapes and pomegranates (the 'Punic apple') on rich estates, guided by Mago's farming manual. They ate puls-like porridge, fish and garum, and Romans copied their recipe for placenta cake.
summary: Destroyed by Rome in the Third Punic War.
government: A republic led by two annually elected suffetes, a council of elders and a popular assembly; Aristotle praised its constitution.
architecture: A circular naval harbour sheltering ~220 warships and tall housing on Byrsa hill.
technology: Shipbuilding with prefabricated, numbered parts, and agriculture described by Mago.
rise: Founded by Phoenicians from Tyre around 814 BCE, it built a trading empire across North Africa, Spain, Sardinia and Sicily.
fall: It lost the three Punic Wars to Rome; in 146 BCE Rome destroyed the city.
legacy: Hannibal's campaign remains a classic of military strategy.
culture: Gods Baal Hammon and Tanit; famous agriculture treatise by Mago.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
known_for: Cyrus's tolerance, the Royal Road, satrapies
life: Farmers paid tribute; craftsmen from across the empire built Persepolis for wages recorded on tablets.
food: Persians ate wheat bread, rice in some regions, mutton, fruit such as pomegranates, apricots and pistachios, and drank wine. Greek writers marvelled at the royal table, which fed up to 15,000 people a day, and at desserts served throughout the meal.
summary: At its height ruled ~44% of the world's population (estimates vary).
government: The 'King of Kings' ruled about 20 satrapies through satraps watched by royal inspectors ('the king's eyes and ears'). Darius I standardised taxes, coinage and laws, while respecting local religions and customs.
architecture: Persepolis with its Apadana audience hall of 72 columns and reliefs of tribute bearers; Pasargadae and Cyrus's tomb.
technology: The 2,700 km Royal Road with relay stations, qanat underground canals, the gold daric coin, and a canal linking the Nile and the Red Sea.
rise: Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes (550 BCE), conquered Lydia and Babylon (539 BCE), and his successors took Egypt and northwest India.
fall: Costly wars with Greece, palace intrigue and revolts weakened it; Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela (331 BCE).
legacy: A model of tolerant, multi-ethnic empire; the Cyrus Cylinder; Persian administrative practices adopted by later empires.
culture: Zoroastrian fire temples, the Nowruz new year, and audience reliefs of 23 nations bringing gifts.

name: Aksum
life: Farmers grew teff and barley; merchants traded ivory and gold to Rome and India.
food: Teff, the tiny grain used for injera flatbread, and barley were staples, with cattle, sheep and honey. Aksum also traded for spices and wine with India and Rome.
summary: One of the four great powers of its time (according to Mani).
government: Aksumite 'kings of kings' ruled vassal states in Ethiopia, Eritrea and at times South Arabia.
architecture: Monolithic stelae up to 33 m tall; one was taken by Italy in 1937 and returned in 2005.
technology: Own gold, silver and bronze coins; terraced farming; Ge'ez script with vowels.
rise: Control of Red Sea trade between Rome, India and Africa made Aksum rich from the 1st century CE.
fall: Islamic control of Red Sea trade, soil exhaustion and climate change led to decline by the 10th century.
legacy: Ethiopian Christianity (from King Ezana, ~330s) and Ge'ez.
culture: Early Christianity, giant stelae and the Ge'ez script still used in Ethiopian liturgy.

name: Ghana Empire
life: Soninke farmers and traders controlled gold coming from the south and salt from the Sahara.
food: People grew millet, sorghum and rice in the Sahel and herded cattle, sheep and goats. Salt, traded from Saharan mines, was so valuable it was exchanged weight for weight with gold in some accounts.
summary: 'Land of gold' for Arab geographers.
government: The king (ghana) ruled from Koumbi Saleh and taxed gold and salt trade; succession passed through the king's sister's son.
architecture: A twin-town capital with a Muslim merchant quarter of stone houses and the royal town.
technology: Organised trans-Saharan caravan trade with camels.
rise: Soninke kings controlled trade between Saharan salt and gold fields of Bambuk from around 300 CE.
fall: Almoravid pressure, drought and shifting trade routes led to decline by 1200.
legacy: West Africa's first great empire; the modern nation of Ghana took its name.
culture: Royal courts with elaborate ceremonies described by Arab geographers.

name: Mali Empire
life: Farmers, herders, fishers and traders lived under clan-based social orders; griots preserved history in song.
food: Mali's farmers grew millet, sorghum and African rice along the Niger, and used shea butter as cooking oil. Ibn Battuta (1352) described millet porridge, fish and baobab sauce.
summary: Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage spread gold through Cairo.
government: The mansa ruled with a council and provincial governors; the Kurukan Fuga charter (1236) traditionally organised clans and rights.
architecture: Mud-brick mosques such as Djinguereber in Timbuktu, designed by the architect Es-Saheli for Mansa Musa.
technology: Manuscript libraries with works on astronomy, medicine and law.
rise: Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at Kirina (1235).
fall: Succession disputes, Tuareg raids and the rise of Songhai.
legacy: Timbuktu's scholarship; the Sundiata epic.
culture: The Sundiata epic, Timbuktu's Sankore university and manuscripts, mud mosques renewed each year.

name: Songhai Empire
life: River fishermen, farmers and merchants along the Niger.
food: Songhai farmers grew rice, millet and sorghum in the Niger bend floodplain; Sorko fishermen supplied fish. Cattle-herding Fulani supplied milk and butter.
summary: Fell to Moroccan musketeers.
government: Askia Muhammad organised provinces, a professional army and Islamic courts.
architecture: The Tomb of Askia in Gao (UNESCO).
technology: A river fleet on the Niger.
rise: Sonni Ali (r. 1464–1492) captured Timbuktu and Djenné.
fall: Moroccan musketeers defeated Songhai at Tondibi in 1591.
legacy: Largest empire in West African history.
culture: Islamic scholarship in Timbuktu and Gao.

name: Great Zimbabwe
life: Cattle herders and farmers; an elite lived inside the stone enclosures.
food: Cattle were the main wealth and source of meat and milk, with sorghum, finger millet and beans grown on hillsides.
summary: Gave its name to modern Zimbabwe.
government: Kings ruled from the Hill Complex; a population of perhaps 10,000–18,000 lived around the stone enclosures.
architecture: Walls up to 11 m high built of granite blocks without mortar, including the Great Enclosure and its conical tower.
technology: Gold mining and trade with the Swahili coast.
rise: Cattle wealth and gold trade from the 11th century.
fall: Overgrazing, depleted resources and shifting trade routes led to abandonment around 1450.
legacy: Colonial authorities long denied Africans built it; it became a symbol of Zimbabwe's independence.
culture: Soapstone bird carvings now on Zimbabwe's flag.

name: Swahili city-states
life: Merchants, sailors and craftsmen in coral-stone towns.
food: Swahili towns ate rice, millet, coconut, bananas, fish and spices traded across the Indian Ocean.
summary: A blend of Bantu, Arab and Persian cultures.
government: Each town had its own sultan and merchant elite.
architecture: Coral-stone mosques and palaces such as Husuni Kubwa at Kilwa.
technology: Dhows sailing with the monsoon to Arabia, India and China.
rise: Bantu coastal communities trading with Arab and Persian merchants from the 8th century.
fall: Portuguese attacks and the shift of trade after 1500.
legacy: The Swahili language, now spoken by about 200 million.
culture: Swahili poetry, Islamic architecture and Indian Ocean dress and food.

name: Kingdom of Benin
life: Guild craftsmen, farmers and court officials lived in a planned walled city.
food: Yams were the central crop, eaten with palm-oil soups, plantains and bushmeat; kola nuts were shared in hospitality.
summary: The British looted the bronzes in 1897; some are now being returned.
government: The Oba ruled with chiefs and guilds of artisans.
architecture: Earthworks around Benin City estimated as among the largest built by people before the mechanical era.
technology: Brass and bronze casting.
rise: Emerged in the forests of southern Nigeria around the 12th century; expanded under Oba Ewuare (~1440).
fall: A British punitive expedition burned the city in 1897.
legacy: The Benin Bronzes, now being returned.
culture: Bronze plaques recording court history; the Igue festival.

name: Ottoman Empire
region: Anatolia, Balkans, Middle East, North Africa
life: Farmers under the timar system, urban guilds, merchants and a multi-faith population organised in millets.
food: Ottoman palace kitchens at Topkapı fed up to 10,000 people a day; dishes included pilaf, kebabs, börek, dolma, yoghurt and baklava. Coffee houses spread from Istanbul in the 16th century.
summary: Lasted over six centuries.
government: The sultan ruled with a grand vizier and the Imperial Council; the devshirme system recruited Christian boys to become janissaries and officials; non-Muslim communities (millets) governed their own religious affairs.
architecture: Mimar Sinan's Süleymaniye and Selimiye mosques, Topkapı Palace and the Blue Mosque.
technology: Large gunpowder artillery (the cannons that breached Constantinople), cartography (Piri Reis's map) and an efficient postal system.
rise: Osman I's frontier principality in Anatolia expanded into the Balkans; Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453; Selim I took Egypt and Arabia; Suleiman reached Vienna (1529).
fall: Military defeats from 1683, nationalism in the Balkans, economic dependence on Europe and defeat in World War I led to its dissolution and the Turkish Republic (1923).
legacy: A multi-faith empire lasting six centuries; modern Middle Eastern and Balkan borders took shape from its collapse.
culture: Coffee houses, Iznik tiles, Sinan's mosques, calligraphy, music and the Turkish bath.

name: Safavid Iran
known_for: Shia Islam as state faith, Isfahan's architecture
life: Silk farmers, carpet weavers and merchants; Isfahan held perhaps half a million people.
food: Rice dishes (polow and chelow) with saffron, herbs and fruit, kebabs, flatbreads and sherbets; tea and coffee spread later.
summary: 'Isfahan is half the world.'
government: Shahs ruled with Qizilbash tribal elites; Shah Abbas I built a slave-soldier army to curb them.
architecture: Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan square, the Shah Mosque and the Si-o-se-pol bridge.
technology: Silk and carpet industries organised for export.
rise: Shah Ismail I founded the dynasty in 1501, making Shia Islam the state religion.
fall: Weak rulers and the Afghan sack of Isfahan in 1722.
legacy: Iran's Shia identity and Persian art.
culture: Miniature painting, carpets, Shia festivals such as Muharram.

name: Indus Valley Civilisation
known_for: Grid cities, drains, standard bricks and weights, undeciphered script
life: Most people farmed or herded; city dwellers worked as potters, bead-makers, metalworkers and traders. Brick houses had wells and bathrooms; children played with clay carts and whistles.
food: Indus farmers grew wheat, barley, millets, peas, lentils, sesame and cotton, and ate dates and mangoes; residues in pots show stews of meat and dairy. Cattle, buffalo, goat and fish were common, and grinding stones, ovens and large granaries suggest organised food storage.
summary: Its cities had some of the best urban drainage of the ancient world.
government: We do not know how the Indus cities were ruled because the script is undeciphered. There are no obvious royal palaces, royal tombs or monuments to rulers, and few weapons. The striking uniformity of brick sizes, weights, seals and city plans over a vast area suggests strong coordination, perhaps by merchant councils, priestly groups or competing elites rather than a single king. Some scholars think it may have been one of history's more egalitarian early civilisations, though this is debated.
architecture: Cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan were laid out in grids, often with a raised 'citadel' and a lower town. Houses of standard-ratio baked bricks (4:2:1) had courtyards, private wells, bathing platforms and latrines connected to covered street drains with manholes. Mohenjo-daro had the Great Bath (12 × 7 m, waterproofed with bitumen), granary-like structures and around 700 wells. Dholavira carved huge rock reservoirs to store rain, and Lothal had a basin interpreted as a dock.
technology: Harappans used a standardised system of cubic chert weights (in a binary-then-decimal series), precise measuring scales, the earliest known cotton cultivation and textiles, drilled carnelian beads with stone drills so fine they remain hard to replicate, bronze tools, wheel-thrown pottery, stoneware bangles, ploughed fields (Kalibangan), and seals carved with animals and script for trade. Dentistry at Mehrgarh, the ancestral site, goes back to ~7000 BCE.
rise: The civilisation grew from farming villages that began at Mehrgarh around 7000 BCE. Over thousands of years villages across the Indus and Ghaggar–Hakra plains grew wheat, barley and cotton and kept humped cattle. Early Harappan towns (~3300–2600 BCE) developed craft traditions and long-distance trade; around 2600 BCE a rapid transformation produced planned cities, writing and standard weights.
fall: From around 1900 BCE the big cities were gradually abandoned and people moved to smaller villages in the east (Haryana, the Ganga–Yamuna doab) and south (Gujarat). The evidence points to a weakening monsoon linked to the 4.2-kiloyear climate event, shifting or drying rivers such as the Ghaggar–Hakra, and the decline of trade with Mesopotamia. The old idea of an 'Aryan invasion' destroying the cities is not supported by evidence; ancient DNA and archaeology show transformation rather than conquest.
legacy: Many elements may have continued into later Indian culture: weights, bangles, cotton weaving, possibly fire rituals, some deities and yoga-like postures on seals, the use of the swastika symbol, bullock carts and farming practices. Most South Asians today carry ancestry from Indus-related people.
culture: Seals with animals and the 'unicorn', terracotta figurines, the Dancing Girl bronze, and possible fire altars at Kalibangan.

name: Vedic India
life: Clans of herders and farmers measured wealth in cattle; later, settled villages grew barley and rice.
food: The Rigvedic diet was based on barley (yava), milk, curd, ghee and honey, with meat at sacrifices; later rice (vrihi) grew in the Ganga valley. Soma, a ritual drink, was praised in hymns.
summary: Foundation of Hindu traditions.
government: Clans (jana) were led by a chief (rajan) whose power was checked by assemblies: the sabha (elders) and samiti (the wider tribe). Priests (purohitas) held great influence through ritual. Over time, clans merged into territorial kingdoms (janapadas) and society hardened into the four varnas.
architecture: Early Vedic people built in wood, thatch and mud, so little survives; archaeologists link the period with Painted Grey Ware sites in the Ganga–Yamuna doab. Fire altars (vedi) were built of bricks to precise geometric plans described in the Shulba Sutras.
technology: The Shulba Sutras (~800–200 BCE) contain geometry for altar construction, including statements of the Pythagorean theorem and approximations of √2. Horse-drawn chariots, iron ploughs in the later period, and an extraordinary oral technology of memorisation preserved the Vedas word-for-word for 3,000 years.
rise: Indo-Aryan-speaking pastoralists, whose ancestry ancient DNA links partly to the steppe, settled in the Punjab (Sapta Sindhu) around 1500 BCE, mixing with local populations descended from Indus-era people. Over centuries they moved east into the Ganga plain, clearing forests with fire and later iron.
fall: The Vedic period did not 'fall' but transformed: by about 600 BCE the clans had become 16 mahajanapadas with cities, coins and kings, and new movements such as Buddhism and Jainism challenged Vedic ritualism.
legacy: The Vedas and Upanishads remain foundational for Hinduism; Sanskrit, ritual traditions, and the concepts of dharma, karma and moksha took shape.
culture: Hymns of the Rigveda, fire sacrifices (yajna), gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna, and the oral tradition that preserved the Vedas.

name: Magadha
known_for: Haryanka, Shishunaga and Nanda dynasties; Buddha and Mahavira's era
life: Rice farmers, ironworkers and traders in a fertile, rising kingdom.
food: Magadha's wealth rested on wet rice cultivation in the Ganga plain, along with pulses, sugarcane and fish.
summary: Became the core of the Mauryan Empire.
government: Magadha's kings, from the Haryanka Bimbisara onward, built a strong monarchy with officials, a standing army and land taxes collected directly.
architecture: Rajagriha (Rajgir) was ringed by 40 km of cyclopean stone walls; Pataliputra, founded by Ajatashatru's successors at the Ganga–Son confluence, became the greatest city of India.
technology: Rich iron mines in the Chota Nagpur region, war elephants from the eastern forests, and new siege weapons described in Buddhist texts gave Magadha a military edge.
rise: Fertile rice land, iron, river trade and capable kings let Magadha conquer Anga, Kosala, Kashi and the Vajji confederacy in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.
fall: It did not fall but became the core of successive empires: the Nandas, Mauryas and Guptas.
legacy: The Buddha and Mahavira taught in Magadha; it was the seed of India's first empire.
culture: Home ground of the Buddha's and Mahavira's teaching; early stupas and viharas.

name: Maurya Empire
known_for: Chandragupta, Chanakya's Arthashastra, Ashoka's edicts and dhamma
life: Farmers paid around a quarter of their harvest in tax; cities had guilds, markets and wooden mansions. Megasthenes described seven social groups and well-run cities.
food: People ate rice, wheat, barley, pulses, sugarcane, dairy and fruit; Megasthenes noted rice eaten from golden bowls. The Arthashastra set rules on storehouses, fair prices and famine relief.
summary: Ashoka turned to Buddhism after Kalinga (261 BCE).
government: The Mauryas built one of the most centralised states of the ancient world. The emperor ruled from Pataliputra with a council of ministers (mantriparishad), with provinces under royal princes at Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri. The Arthashastra, attributed to Chanakya (Kautilya), describes departments for revenue, mines, trade, weights, forests, elephants and a network of spies. Megasthenes, the Seleucid ambassador, reported city boards managing trade, foreigners, births and deaths, and an army of perhaps 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants (likely exaggerated). Ashoka added dhamma-mahamattas, officials to promote ethics, welfare and religious harmony.
architecture: Pataliputra was protected by a timber palisade about 14 km long with 570 towers, and had a pillared palace hall at Kumrahar. Ashoka erected polished sandstone pillars topped with animal capitals, such as the Lion Capital of Sarnath (India's national emblem), built thousands of stupas including the core of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, and cut the earliest rock-cut caves at Barabar for the Ajivika sect.
technology: The Mauryas built a royal highway (Uttarapatha) from Taxila to Pataliputra and on toward Bengal, with trees, wells and rest houses that Ashoka describes in his edicts. They operated state mines, mints for punch-marked silver coins, irrigation such as the Sudarshana lake in Gujarat, shipbuilding and a polished stone-working technique (the 'Mauryan polish') that still gleams. Ashoka's edicts were the first large body of written Indian texts, in Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts.
rise: Chandragupta Maurya, advised by the Brahmin strategist Chanakya, overthrew the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 322 BCE, after Alexander's withdrawal from Punjab left a power vacuum in the northwest. In about 303 BCE he defeated or made peace with Seleucus I, gaining Afghanistan and Baluchistan in exchange for 500 war elephants. His son Bindusara expanded into the Deccan, and Ashoka conquered Kalinga (261 BCE), bringing almost the whole subcontinent except the far south under one rule.
fall: After Ashoka's death in 232 BCE the empire split between successors, provinces broke away, and revenue fell. Some historians blame the costs of a vast bureaucracy and army; others cite Ashoka's pacifism weakening the military, though this is disputed. In 185 BCE the general Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, during an army review and founded the Shunga dynasty, while Indo-Greeks invaded from the northwest.
legacy: The first empire to unite most of South Asia; Ashoka's edicts on tolerance, non-violence and welfare; the spread of Buddhism to Sri Lanka, Central Asia and later East Asia; the national emblem and the Ashoka Chakra on India's flag; and the Arthashastra's political thought.
culture: Ashoka's dhamma, Buddhist missions to Sri Lanka and beyond, polished stone pillars and the Sanchi stupa.

name: Satavahana dynasty
life: Deccan farmers and merchants trading with Rome; Buddhist monasteries supported by traders.
food: Rice in coastal areas, millets in the Deccan, pulses and dairy; pepper and textiles were exported to Rome.
summary: Issued coins with kings' portraits.
government: Kings ruled the Deccan through feudatories (maharathis) and queens sometimes acted as regents; inscriptions name kings with their mothers' names (e.g. Gautamiputra Satakarni).
architecture: The chaitya hall at Karla, the caves at Nashik and Bhaja, and the richly carved stupa at Amaravati.
technology: Coins with ships show maritime trade; they issued lead and potin coins and controlled ports for Roman trade.
rise: After the Mauryas declined, Simuka founded the dynasty around the 1st century BCE in the western Deccan.
fall: Wars with the Western Kshatrapas and internal division split the realm into smaller kingdoms by the early 3rd century.
legacy: Linked north and south India; patrons of Prakrit literature such as the Gatha Saptashati and of Buddhist art.
culture: Amaravati sculpture and Karla caves.

name: Sangam-era Tamilakam
known_for: Chera, Chola, Pandya kingdoms; Sangam poetry
life: People lived by five landscapes (tinai): hills, forests, farmland, coast and desert, each with its own work and gods.
food: Tamils ate rice, millet, fish, meat and fruit; Sangam poems describe five landscapes each with its own food. Black pepper was exported to Rome.
summary: Sangam poems describe love and war across five landscapes.
government: Three crowned dynasties, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, ruled with numerous chieftains (velir); bards and poets were honoured at court and assemblies (manram) settled disputes.
architecture: Brick towns with drainage and wells at Keeladi, port cities such as Kaveripattinam and Muziris, and memorial hero-stones (natukal).
technology: Iron smelting (iron furnaces and steel), a Tamil-Brahmi script found even on everyday pottery at Keeladi suggesting widespread literacy, and long-distance shipping to Rome and Southeast Asia.
rise: Iron Age farming and port trade with the Romans and Greeks enriched the Tamil coast from about the 3rd century BCE.
fall: The obscure Kalabhra period (~3rd–6th century) displaced the three dynasties until the Pallavas and Pandyas revived.
legacy: Over 2,000 Sangam poems, the Tirukkural and the foundation of Tamil literary culture.
culture: Sangam love and war poetry (akam and puram), hero stones, Murugan worship.

name: Kushan Empire
life: A mix of nomad elites, farmers and Silk Road merchants.
food: Wheat, barley, grapes, melons and wine in Bactria; rice and dairy in India.
summary: Spread Mahayana Buddhism to Central Asia.
government: Kushan emperors such as Kanishka called themselves 'son of heaven' (devaputra) and 'king of kings', ruling through satraps from Bactria to the Ganga.
architecture: Buddhist stupas and monasteries of Gandhara and Mathura, and the giant Kanishka stupa at Peshawar.
technology: They issued abundant gold coins and controlled the Silk Road's southern branches, linking Rome, Persia, India and China.
rise: The Yuezhi nomads, pushed from China's frontier, conquered Bactria; Kujula Kadphises united them in the 1st century CE.
fall: Defeats by the Sasanians in the 3rd century and the rise of the Guptas in India reduced them to minor rulers.
legacy: Gandhara art made the first human images of the Buddha; Mahayana Buddhism spread along their trade routes to China.
culture: Gandhara and Mathura art made the first Buddha images in human form.

name: Gupta Empire
known_for: Golden age of science and art: zero, Aryabhata, Kalidasa
life: Prosperous farmers and guilds; Faxian described peaceful towns and free hospitals.
food: Rice, wheat, pulses, milk products, sugar (crystallised sugar was an Indian invention) and spices; Faxian noted that many people avoided meat, onions and alcohol.
summary: Weakened by Huna invasions.
government: The Guptas ruled the Ganga heartland directly but most of their empire through feudatories and tributary kings who acknowledged their supremacy. Kings took grand titles such as Maharajadhiraja. Land grants to Brahmins and temples, recorded on copper plates, began a process of decentralisation. Faxian, a Chinese monk who visited around 400 CE, described light taxes, few death penalties and rest houses and free hospitals in the towns.
architecture: Gupta builders made some of the earliest free-standing stone Hindu temples, such as the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh and the temple at Bhitargaon in brick, the Udayagiri caves with the great boar (Varaha) relief, Buddhist sculpture at Sarnath, and the paintings of Ajanta (under the contemporary Vakatakas). The Delhi Iron Pillar, over 7 m tall and nearly rust-free after 1,600 years, was made in this era.
technology: Indian mathematics and astronomy reached a peak: Aryabhata (476–550) proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis, explained eclipses, calculated π as 3.1416 and used place value; the decimal system with zero was being developed (formalised by Brahmagupta in 628). Medicine (Sushruta and Charaka traditions), metallurgy, textile dyeing and Sanskrit grammar flourished. Nalanda university was founded under Kumaragupta I.
rise: The Guptas began as a minor family in Magadha. Chandragupta I (r. ~320–335) married Kumaradevi, a princess of the powerful Licchavi clan, which raised his status. His son Samudragupta (r. ~335–375), celebrated in the Allahabad pillar inscription, conquered or subdued kings across northern India and received tribute from the south. Chandragupta II (r. ~375–415) defeated the Western Kshatrapas, gaining Gujarat's sea trade.
fall: From around 460 CE the Alchon Huns (Hunas) invaded from Central Asia. Skandagupta repelled them at first, but later attacks under Toramana and Mihirakula devastated the northwest and drained the treasury. At the same time feudatories such as the Maukharis and Maitrakas became independent, trade with the Roman world declined, and the dynasty faded by around 550.
legacy: Called India's 'Classical' or 'Golden Age': Kalidasa's plays and poems, the Puranas compiled, temple architecture, decimal mathematics with zero that later spread to the Arab world and Europe, and art styles that influenced Southeast and East Asia.
culture: Kalidasa's drama, Ajanta murals, temple building, Sanskrit learning and the Puranas.

name: Pallava dynasty
life: Farmers in the Kaveri and Palar basins; port trade from Mamallapuram.
food: Rice, millets, coconuts, pepper and fish.
summary: Spread Indian scripts to Southeast Asia.
government: Pallava kings ruled from Kanchipuram with ministers and village assemblies, using Sanskrit and Tamil.
architecture: The rock-cut monuments of Mamallapuram, including the Shore Temple, the Pancha Rathas and the giant relief 'Arjuna's Penance', and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram.
technology: Developed the Pallava–Grantha script, ancestor of many Southeast Asian scripts.
rise: Rose in the 3rd–4th centuries around Kanchipuram after the Satavahanas.
fall: Defeated by the Cholas around 897.
legacy: The foundation of Dravidian temple architecture.
culture: Rock-cut temples and the bhakti poetry of the Alvars and Nayanars.

name: Chalukya dynasty
known_for: Rock-cut temples at Badami, Aihole, Pattadakal
life: Farmers and traders of the Deccan plateau.
food: Millets (jowar, ragi), rice and pulses.
summary: Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha.
government: The Badami Chalukyas ruled the Deccan through feudatories; Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha on the Narmada around 618.
architecture: Cave temples at Badami, the experimental temples of Aihole, and the UNESCO group at Pattadakal blending northern and southern styles.
technology: Advanced stone carving and temple engineering.
rise: Pulakeshin I founded Badami as capital in 543.
fall: The Rashtrakutas overthrew them in 753; a later branch ruled from Kalyani.
legacy: The Vesara temple style and Kannada inscriptions.
culture: Temple experiments mixing northern and southern styles at Pattadakal.

name: Rashtrakuta dynasty
life: An agrarian empire of the Deccan with powerful feudatories.
food: Jowar and other millets, rice, pulses and dairy.
summary: Arab travellers ranked its king among the world's four greatest.
government: A powerful Deccan monarchy; Arab traveller Sulaiman listed its king among the four great rulers of the world.
architecture: The Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single rock by removing about 200,000 tonnes of stone.
technology: Masterful rock-cut engineering.
rise: Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukyas in 753.
fall: Western Chalukyas defeated them in 982.
legacy: Kannada literature (Kavirajamarga) and Ellora.
culture: Kannada literature and the Ellora Kailasa temple.

name: Chola Empire
region: South India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia
known_for: Brihadeeswara temple, bronzes, navy, village self-government
life: Rice farmers under elected village assemblies; temple towns employed dancers, musicians and craftsmen.
food: Rice from the Kaveri delta, coconut, tamarind, pepper and fish; temple kitchens served thousands.
summary: Rajendra I raided Srivijaya in 1025.
government: The Chola king ruled through a hierarchy of provinces (mandalams), districts (valanadus) and village groups (nadus), but villages enjoyed remarkable self-government. Inscriptions at Uttaramerur (~919–921 CE) describe village assemblies (sabhas) choosing committee members by lottery (kudavolai, 'pot ticket') from qualified candidates, with rules disqualifying the corrupt and their relatives. Temples were economic hubs, employing hundreds of people and lending money.
architecture: The Cholas built some of India's greatest temples: the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur (1010), whose granite tower rises about 66 m and is crowned by an 80-tonne capstone; the temple of Gangaikonda Cholapuram; and Airavatesvara at Darasuram, all UNESCO World Heritage sites. They also built tanks, irrigation channels and maintained the ancient Kallanai dam on the Kaveri.
technology: Chola artisans perfected lost-wax bronze casting, producing the iconic Nataraja (Shiva as cosmic dancer). Engineers moved and raised enormous granite blocks, built irrigation systems in the Kaveri delta, and the navy mastered the monsoon winds to sail to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Southeast Asia. Land surveys under Rajaraja I recorded tax for every village.
rise: The early Cholas appear in Sangam literature, but the Imperial Cholas began when Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars around 848. Rajaraja I (985–1014) conquered the Cheras, Pandyas, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives; his son Rajendra I (1014–1044) marched to the Ganga, founding Gangaikonda Cholapuram ('city of the Chola who conquered the Ganga'), and sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya empire in 1025.
fall: Long wars with the Western Chalukyas drained resources. In the 12th–13th centuries, provincial chiefs grew powerful, the Pandyas revived in the south and the Hoysalas in the west. The last Chola king, Rajendra III, was defeated by the Pandya Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan around 1279.
legacy: Dravidian temple architecture, Chola bronzes, the spread of Tamil culture and Hindu-Buddhist influence to Southeast Asia, and an early example of local democratic administration.
culture: Bronze Nataraja, temple festivals, Tamil devotional poetry and Bharatanatyam roots.

name: Pala Empire
life: Rice farmers and traders of Bengal and Bihar.
food: Rice, fish, pulses and sweets made from milk.
summary: Last great Buddhist empire in India.
government: Founded by Gopala, elected by local chiefs to end anarchy (matsyanyaya, 'law of the fishes'); later kings were Buddhist patrons with feudatory chiefs.
architecture: The Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur (Bangladesh), one of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalaya.
technology: Pala bronze and stone sculpture and palm-leaf manuscript painting.
rise: Gopala's election around 750; Dharmapala and Devapala expanded the realm across north India.
fall: Weakened by Pratihara and Rashtrakuta wars, they were overthrown by the Senas in the 12th century.
legacy: Nalanda and Vikramashila universities; Pala art shaped Tibetan Buddhism.
culture: Buddhist universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila and Pala sculpture.

name: Delhi Sultanate
known_for: Qutub Minar, Persian culture, iqta system
life: Peasant villages paid revenue to iqta holders; cities grew with Persian-speaking elites and Indian artisans.
food: Wheat bread, rice, meat dishes such as samosa (sanbusa) and pilaf, and sweets; Persian cuisine mixed with Indian.
summary: Razia Sultan was its only woman ruler.
government: Sultans ruled with Turkic, Afghan and later Indian nobles who received iqtas (revenue assignments) in return for military service. Alauddin Khalji controlled market prices, measured land and built a large standing army to repel Mongols; Muhammad bin Tughlaq experimented boldly with token copper currency and moving the capital to Daulatabad, with disastrous results.
architecture: The Sultanate introduced the true arch and dome to India: the Qutub Minar (72.5 m), the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Alai Darwaza, the fortress cities of Tughlaqabad and Siri, and the tombs of the Lodis in Delhi.
technology: Paper, the Persian wheel for irrigation, the spinning wheel, gunpowder (late), and new building techniques arrived or spread; Persian became the language of administration.
rise: Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain (1192); after his death his slave general Qutb ud-Din Aibak ruled from Delhi (1206). Five dynasties followed: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi.
fall: Overexpansion, rebellions in Bengal and the Deccan, the founding of the Bahmani and Vijayanagara states, Timur's devastating sack of Delhi (1398), and finally Babur's victory over Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat (1526).
legacy: Indo-Islamic architecture, the Hindustani language, Sufi orders, and repelling the Mongols from India.
culture: Sufi shrines, qawwali (Amir Khusrau), Indo-Islamic architecture and the birth of Hindustani.

name: Vijayanagara Empire
life: Farmers, temple communities and merchants; Hampi's bazaars sold rubies and horses.
food: Rice, ragi, pulses and spices; Domingo Paes described markets full of food.
summary: Defeated at Talikota (1565).
government: Kings ruled through nayakas, military chiefs given territory (amaram) in return for troops, a system later continued by the Nayaka kingdoms of Madurai and Thanjavur. Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529) was a great general, administrator and poet.
architecture: The capital Hampi had massive walls, the Virupaksha and Vittala temples (with musical pillars and the stone chariot), the Lotus Mahal, elephant stables, stepped tanks and aqueducts across a landscape of giant granite boulders.
technology: Advanced water engineering with tanks, canals and aqueducts; large armies using cavalry and later firearms; a busy trade in diamonds, spices and horses.
rise: Brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family founded the empire in 1336 to resist the Delhi Sultanate's raids into the south.
fall: An alliance of the Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565; Hampi was sacked for months. The dynasty continued weakly until 1646.
legacy: Carnatic music (Purandara Dasa), Telugu and Kannada literature and the UNESCO ruins of Hampi.
culture: Mahanavami festival, Carnatic music and Telugu and Kannada poetry.

name: Ahom kingdom
known_for: Resisted the Mughals for centuries; Lachit Borphukan at Saraighat (1671)
life: Wet-rice farmers organised by the paik labour system.
food: Rice, fish, bamboo shoots and rice beer.
summary: Lasted nearly 600 years.
government: The Ahom king (swargadeo) ruled with great ministers (gohains) and the paik system, in which every adult male owed labour or military service in rotation.
architecture: Rang Ghar, Asia's oldest surviving amphitheatre pavilion, the Talatal Ghar palace and the maidam burial mounds of Charaideo (UNESCO, 2024).
technology: Gunpowder and cannon, river naval warfare, and embankments along the Brahmaputra.
rise: The Tai prince Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills in 1228 and united local peoples.
fall: Civil war, Burmese invasions (1817–1826) and British annexation after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826).
legacy: Repelled the Mughals at Saraighat (1671); Assamese identity and the Buranji chronicles.
culture: Buranji chronicles and Bihu festivities.

name: Mughal Empire
known_for: Akbar, Taj Mahal, miniature painting, Persianate culture
life: Most people were peasants paying a third or more of their harvest; cities held weavers, merchants and nobles' households.
food: Mughal kitchens blended Persian, Central Asian and Indian cooking: biryani, pulao, kebabs, kormas, naan and kulfi. Babur missed Kabul's melons; ordinary people ate khichdi, roti and dal.
summary: Ended after the 1857 uprising.
government: The emperor held absolute power, supported by the mansabdari system: nobles (mansabdars) held numbered ranks determining their salary and the cavalry they must supply, and were paid through revenue assignments (jagirs) that were regularly transferred to prevent local power bases. Akbar's finance minister Raja Todar Mal measured land and fixed tax as a share of average produce (the zabt system). Akbar also abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, took Rajput nobles into high office and promoted sulh-i-kul, 'peace with all'.
architecture: Mughal architecture blended Persian, Timurid and Indian traditions: Humayun's Tomb (1570) with its charbagh garden; Akbar's red sandstone city of Fatehpur Sikri and Agra Fort; Jahangir's gardens in Kashmir; and under Shah Jahan, the white-marble Taj Mahal (1632–1653), the Red Fort and Jama Masjid of Delhi. Pietra dura inlay, domes, arches, minarets and symmetrical gardens defined the style.
technology: The Mughals used gunpowder artillery and matchlock muskets (Babur won at Panipat with Ottoman-style tactics), built a road network with sarais, minted high-quality silver rupees (a standard introduced by Sher Shah Suri), and supported astronomy and the production of world-leading textiles. The Mughal economy produced roughly a quarter of world output around 1700 by Angus Maddison's estimates.
rise: Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527). His son Humayun lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (1540) and regained it in 1555. Akbar (r. 1556–1605) won the Second Battle of Panipat and built a stable empire through conquest, alliances and reforms.
fall: Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) expanded the empire to its largest extent but spent 25 years at war in the Deccan against the Marathas, emptying the treasury, while reimposing the jizya alienated many subjects. After his death, wars of succession, rebellious governors (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), Maratha expansion, Sikh and Jat revolts, Nadir Shah's devastating sack of Delhi (1739) and Afghan invasions shattered central power. The East India Company reduced the emperors to pensioners, and the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled after 1857.
legacy: Indo-Persian architecture, Mughlai cuisine, miniature painting, Hindustani music and the Urdu language, administrative practices adopted by the British, and the idea of a pan-Indian state.
culture: Miniature painting, Persian and Urdu poetry, Hindustani music, gardens, and cuisine such as biryani.

name: Maratha Confederacy
life: Deccan peasants, soldiers and hill-fort garrisons.
food: Bhakri of jowar or bajra, dal, onion and chillies — a portable diet for fast cavalry.
summary: Became the dominant Indian power in the 18th century.
government: Shivaji created a council of eight ministers (Ashta Pradhan), paid soldiers in cash rather than land grants, and collected chauth (a quarter of revenue) and sardeshmukhi from neighbouring territories. Under the Peshwas (prime ministers) from 1713, power shifted to Pune, and great chiefs (Holkar, Scindia, Gaekwad, Bhonsle) formed a confederacy.
architecture: Hundreds of hill and sea forts such as Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad and Sindhudurg; the Peshwas' Shaniwar Wada in Pune; and temples and ghats across India restored by Ahilyabai Holkar.
technology: Guerrilla tactics (ganimi kava) suited to mountains; a navy under Kanhoji Angre that challenged the British and Portuguese; and later European-trained artillery under Mahadji Scindia.
rise: Shivaji (1630–1680) built a state in the Western Ghats by seizing Bijapur forts, defeated Afzal Khan (1659), escaped from Aurangzeb's custody at Agra (1666) and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. After Aurangzeb's death the Marathas expanded across India under Peshwa Bajirao I.
fall: Defeat by Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) cost a generation of leaders. Internal rivalries let the British win three Anglo-Maratha Wars; the confederacy ended in 1818.
legacy: A powerful symbol of regional pride and resistance; the Maratha navy, Marathi culture and much of central India's princely history.
culture: Bhakti saints like Tukaram and festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi.

name: Sikh Empire
life: Punjabi farmers and soldiers in a multi-faith state.
food: Wheat roti, dairy, and the langar community kitchen that fed everyone equally.
summary: Annexed by the East India Company in 1849.
government: Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled a secular state in which Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims served in high office; his Khalsa army was modernised by European officers.
architecture: He gilded the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple), and built Lahore's palaces and the gurdwara at the Guru's birthplace.
technology: A modern artillery corps and infantry trained on European lines.
rise: Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh misls and captured Lahore in 1799, then Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar.
fall: After his death in 1839, court intrigue and assassinations weakened the state; the British won the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–46, 1848–49) and annexed Punjab.
legacy: The memory of Sikh sovereignty and the Golden Temple's golden dome; the Koh-i-Noor was taken to Britain.
culture: Gurdwara langar, Baisakhi and the gilding of the Golden Temple.

name: Kingdom of Mysore
known_for: Hyder Ali, Tipu Sultan's war rockets
life: Farmers and silk weavers; artisans for the court.
food: Ragi balls (ragi mudde), rice and sambar.
summary: Tipu's Mysorean rockets influenced British rocketry.
government: Ruled by the Wodeyar family from 1399; Hyder Ali, a commander, took power in 1761, and his son Tipu Sultan modernised revenue, trade and the army.
architecture: Srirangapatna fort, Tipu's Daria Daulat Bagh summer palace and later the Mysore Palace.
technology: Iron-cased Mysorean rockets used against the British, which inspired the British Congreve rocket; silk farming introduced by Tipu.
rise: Hyder Ali seized power from the Wodeyars and expanded Mysore across the south.
fall: Four Anglo-Mysore Wars; Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the British restored the Wodeyars as subordinate rulers.
legacy: Rocketry and Mysore Dasara.
culture: Mysore Dasara and Mysore painting.

name: East India Company rule
life: Peasants paid high land revenue; weavers lost markets to British cloth.
food: Indians ate traditional grains and pulses, but Company revenue demands contributed to famines such as the Bengal famine of 1770, which killed about a third of the province's people.
summary: A private company ruled India with its own army of ~260,000.
government: A joint-stock company governed by directors in London, supervised from 1773 by Parliament, ruled through a Governor-General in Calcutta and presidencies in Madras and Bombay, with a private army of Indian sepoys.
architecture: Fort William in Calcutta, Fort St George in Madras and neo-classical government buildings.
technology: Surveys such as the Great Trigonometrical Survey (from 1802), which later measured Everest; steamships and the first telegraph lines.
rise: Victory at Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) turned the Company into a territorial power; wars against Mysore, the Marathas and Sikhs extended its rule.
fall: The 1857 uprising led Parliament to abolish Company rule in 1858.
legacy: Colonial administration, the drain of wealth, and the deindustrialisation of Indian textiles.
culture: Company paintings and early printing presses in Calcutta.

name: British Raj
life: Most Indians remained farmers facing famines; cities grew with mills, railways and an English-educated middle class.
food: Most Indians ate rice or wheat, pulses and vegetables; famines in 1876–78, 1896–1902 and 1943 killed tens of millions while grain was exported.
summary: Ended with Independence and Partition in 1947.
government: India was ruled by a Viceroy responsible to the Secretary of State in London; about 1,000 Indian Civil Service officers governed 300 million people. About 560 princely states remained under indirect rule. Limited reforms (1909, 1919, 1935) gave Indians some elected seats.
architecture: New Delhi by Lutyens and Baker, Indo-Saracenic buildings such as Victoria Terminus (Mumbai) and the Victoria Memorial (Kolkata), hill stations and cantonments.
technology: About 67,000 km of railways, telegraph, canals in Punjab, and the census; but designed largely to serve British commercial and military needs.
rise: After 1857 the British Crown took direct control (1858); Victoria became Empress of India in 1877.
fall: The mass freedom movement led by Gandhi, Nehru, Bose, Patel and many others, the 1946 naval mutiny, Britain's exhaustion after WWII, and the end of Indian soldiers' loyalty led to independence and Partition on 15 August 1947.
legacy: Parliamentary institutions, English as a link language and railways, but also famines, poverty, communal division and Partition.
culture: The Bengal Renaissance, new Indian newspapers, and the rise of nationalism.

name: Xia and Shang China
life: Millet farmers, bronze casters and diviners lived around royal centres.
food: Millet in the north and rice in the south, plus pigs, dogs and fermented alcoholic drinks made in bronze vessels.
summary: The earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones.
government: Shang kings ruled with the help of ancestors, consulted through divination; they led armies, performed sacrifices (including human sacrifice) and controlled bronze production.
architecture: The capital Yin (Anyang) had rammed-earth palace foundations and royal tombs; Erlitou (possibly Xia) had the earliest palaces in China.
technology: Sophisticated bronze casting with piece-moulds, horse-drawn chariots, silk and the oracle-bone script, ancestor of Chinese characters.
rise: The Shang overthrew the semi-legendary Xia around 1600 BCE according to tradition.
fall: The last Shang king, remembered as a tyrant, was defeated by the Zhou around 1046 BCE.
legacy: Writing, bronze art and ancestor veneration that shaped Chinese civilisation.
culture: Ancestor worship and oracle-bone divination.

name: Zhou dynasty
life: Peasants worked land for lords under a feudal order.
food: Millet, wheat, soybeans, vegetables and meat for nobles; elaborate ritual banquets were described in the Book of Rites.
summary: China's longest dynasty.
government: The Western Zhou kings granted land to relatives and allies in a feudal system, justified by the Mandate of Heaven: heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants. After 771 BCE royal power faded and states competed in the Spring and Autumn (770–476) and Warring States (475–221) periods.
architecture: Walled cities, ancestral temples and elaborate ritual bronze vessels with long inscriptions.
technology: Iron tools and casting, the crossbow, cavalry, and large irrigation works such as Dujiangyan (256 BCE), still in use.
rise: King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at Muye around 1046 BCE.
fall: Nomad attacks and rebellion forced the move east in 771 BCE; afterwards the Zhou kings were figureheads until Qin extinguished them in 256 BCE.
legacy: Confucius, Laozi, Mencius and Sunzi lived in the Zhou era, the classical age of Chinese philosophy.
culture: Confucian rites, the Book of Songs and Taoist ideas.

name: Qin dynasty
known_for: Unification, the Terracotta Army, standard script
life: Peasants were conscripted for armies and huge building projects.
food: Millet and wheat, with state granaries feeding armies.
summary: Gave China its name.
government: Qin Shi Huang ruled by Legalist principles: strict laws, harsh punishments, collective responsibility, and abolition of feudal fiefs in favour of 36 commanderies run by appointed officials.
architecture: The emperor's tomb near Xi'an, guarded by about 8,000 life-size terracotta soldiers, horses and chariots; the first connected Great Wall; and the vast Epang Palace.
technology: The Qin standardised script, coins, weights, measures and axle widths, built about 6,800 km of roads and the Lingqu canal linking the Yangtze and Pearl river systems, and mass-produced crossbows with interchangeable parts.
rise: Qin, a western state, became powerful after Shang Yang's Legalist reforms (4th century BCE). King Ying Zheng conquered the other six Warring States by 221 BCE and named himself First Emperor.
fall: Massive forced labour, harsh laws and book burning provoked hatred. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, the Chen Sheng–Wu Guang uprising and other rebellions brought down the dynasty by 206 BCE.
legacy: The name 'China' probably comes from Qin; the unified written language and centralised state lasted two millennia.
culture: Standardised writing and legalist philosophy.

name: Han dynasty
known_for: Paper, the Silk Road, Confucian civil service
life: Peasant families farmed with iron ploughs; officials studied Confucian classics.
food: Millet, wheat (as noodles), rice, soybeans and tofu (traditionally Han), plus pork and tea.
summary: Han is still the name of China's majority people.
government: The Han combined Qin centralisation with Confucian ideals. Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BCE) made Confucianism the state ideology and founded an Imperial Academy; officials were recommended for virtue and tested on the classics. Commanderies and counties were run by appointed officials, with state monopolies on salt and iron to raise revenue.
architecture: Han cities such as Chang'an and Luoyang had walled palaces and markets; tombs held clay models of houses, watchtowers and farms showing everyday buildings. The Han extended the Great Wall west into the Gansu corridor to protect Silk Road trade.
technology: Cai Lun refined papermaking around 105 CE; Zhang Heng built a seismoscope (132 CE) and a water-powered armillary sphere; the Han also developed the wheelbarrow, blast furnaces producing cast iron, the rudder, the horse collar and acupuncture texts.
rise: Liu Bang, a peasant-born official, rebelled after the Qin collapse and defeated the aristocrat Xiang Yu in 202 BCE, founding the Han. He softened Qin's harsh laws while keeping its centralised structure.
fall: Land concentration, court intrigue between eunuchs and consort families, and natural disasters led to the Yellow Turban rebellion (184 CE). Warlords who suppressed it carved up China; in 220 the last Han emperor abdicated, beginning the Three Kingdoms.
legacy: The Han defined Chinese identity; the majority ethnic group still calls itself Han. Paper, the Silk Road and the Confucian civil service were its lasting gifts.
culture: Silk, lacquer, paper and the historian Sima Qian.

name: Tang dynasty
life: Chang'an was a cosmopolitan city of about a million.
food: Rice, wheat cakes, mutton and tea, which became a national drink; foreign foods such as grapes and sesame cakes were popular in Chang'an.
summary: A golden age of Chinese culture.
government: The Tang emperor ruled through the Three Departments and Six Ministries: a Secretariat drafted edicts, a Chancellery reviewed them, and the Department of State Affairs carried them out through ministries of personnel, revenue, rites, war, justice and works. Officials were increasingly chosen by competitive imperial examinations on the Confucian classics and poetry. The 'equal-field' system allotted land to peasant households in return for taxes in grain and cloth and labour service, and the Tang Code (624) became the model for law across East Asia. Wu Zetian (r. 690–705) became China's only woman emperor in her own name.
architecture: Chang'an, the capital, was the largest city in the world (~1 million people), laid out on a strict grid of 108 walled wards around a central avenue 150 m wide, with two great markets where Persians, Sogdians, Arabs and Indians traded. The Tang built the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda to house sutras brought from India by Xuanzang, the vast Daming Palace, Buddhist cave temples at Longmen and Dunhuang, and wooden halls that influenced Japanese temples like those of Nara.
technology: The Tang produced the world's oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra (868), by woodblock printing; early porcelain and sancai three-colour glazed ceramics; mechanical clocks with water-driven escapements; advances in medicine (Sun Simiao's encyclopaedias), cartography and astronomy (Yi Xing measured the meridian). Alchemists experimenting with saltpetre and sulphur took the first steps toward gunpowder.
rise: After the short Sui dynasty reunified China (581) but exhausted it with huge canal projects and failed wars in Korea, rebellions broke out. Li Yuan, a Sui general, and his son Li Shimin captured Chang'an and founded the Tang in 618. Li Shimin, as Emperor Taizong (r. 626–649), defeated the Eastern Turks, extended control along the Silk Road into Central Asia, and governed so effectively his reign became a byword for good rule.
fall: In 751 the Tang lost to the Abbasids at the Battle of Talas, ending expansion westward. In 755 the general An Lushan rebelled; the eight-year An Lushan rebellion devastated the north and may have cost millions of lives. Afterwards provincial military governors (jiedushi) became semi-independent, eunuchs dominated the court, and the equal-field system collapsed. The Huang Chao rebellion (874–884) sacked Chang'an, and in 907 the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, opening the Five Dynasties period.
legacy: The Tang is regarded as a high point of Chinese civilisation: the golden age of poetry (Li Bai, Du Fu, Wang Wei), Chan (Zen) Buddhism, a cosmopolitan culture, and institutions copied by Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Overseas Chinese still call themselves 'people of Tang'.
culture: Poetry of Li Bai and Du Fu, tea culture and Buddhist art.

name: Song dynasty
known_for: Gunpowder weapons, compass, movable type, paper money
life: Commercial towns, rice farmers and scholar-officials.
food: Champa rice, tea, restaurants and teahouses in cities; the first known restaurant menus.
summary: The world's most advanced economy of its time.
government: The Song placed civilian scholar-officials above generals, recruiting them through greatly expanded examinations. Reformers like Wang Anshi tried state loans to farmers and new taxes; Neo-Confucian thinkers like Zhu Xi reshaped education.
architecture: Song builders wrote the Yingzao Fashi construction manual (1103), built tall pagodas and covered bridges, and laid out bustling commercial cities like Kaifeng, shown in the scroll 'Along the River During the Qingming Festival'.
technology: The Song had the world's most advanced economy: gunpowder weapons and fire lances, the magnetic compass for navigation, movable type (Bi Sheng, ~1040), the first government paper money (jiaozi), large ocean-going junks with watertight bulkheads, and new rice varieties from Champa that doubled harvests.
rise: General Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 960 and reunified most of China, ending the Five Dynasties chaos.
fall: The Song lost the north to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 and moved its capital to Hangzhou. The Mongols conquered the Jin, then besieged Song cities for decades; the last Song emperor died at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279.
legacy: Printing, the compass and gunpowder spread from Song China to the world; Song landscape painting and porcelain set lasting standards.
culture: Landscape painting, printed books and the tea house.

name: Yuan dynasty
life: Mongol, Chinese and foreign populations under a layered order.
food: Mongol mutton, dairy and soups combined with Chinese rice dishes.
summary: Founded by Genghis Khan's grandson.
government: Kublai Khan ruled China as Great Khan and Emperor, dividing society into four ranks: Mongols, Semu (Central Asians and others), northern Chinese and southern Chinese. The examination system was suspended until 1315 and many officials were foreigners, among them Persians, Uyghurs and, by his own account, Marco Polo.
architecture: The new capital Dadu (Khanbaliq, today's Beijing) was laid out on a classical grid with palaces, lakes and the White Pagoda, built by the Nepali architect Araniko.
technology: Paper money circulated empire-wide. The Grand Canal was extended to Beijing. Guo Shoujing built observatories and calculated the year to within 26 seconds. Postal relay stations (yam) linked China to Persia.
rise: Genghis Khan's Mongols attacked the Jin from 1211. His grandson Kublai declared the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and destroyed the Southern Song in 1279, the first time a non-Chinese people ruled all of China.
fall: Failed invasions of Japan (1274, 1281) and Java drained the treasury, and paper-money inflation and Yellow River floods followed. Plague and ethnic discrimination fuelled the Red Turban revolts. Zhu Yuanzhang took Dadu in 1368 and the Mongols withdrew to the steppe.
