legacy: It reunified China after centuries of division and opened the age of Silk Road contact with Europe described by Marco Polo. It also produced zaju drama.
culture: Yuan drama and blue-and-white porcelain.

name: Ming dynasty
known_for: Forbidden City, Zheng He's voyages, porcelain
life: A large farming population and busy market towns.
food: Rice and new American crops: maize, sweet potatoes and chillies.
summary: Rebuilt the Great Wall in stone.
government: The founding emperor Hongwu abolished the post of chancellor and ruled personally through ministries, with a secret police (the Embroidered Uniform Guard). Later emperors relied heavily on eunuchs. The examination system and the eight-legged essay dominated elite life.
architecture: The Ming built the Forbidden City in Beijing (1406–1420), the Temple of Heaven, the Ming tombs and rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and stone into the form seen today.
technology: Zheng He's treasure fleets (1405–1433) sailed ships far larger than European vessels to India, Arabia and East Africa. The Ming produced famous blue-and-white porcelain, encyclopaedias like the Yongle Encyclopedia, and adopted New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes.
rise: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant orphan and former monk, led the Red Turban rebellion against the Mongol Yuan and founded the Ming in 1368.
fall: Bureaucratic paralysis, eunuch corruption, costly wars in Korea against Japan, silver shortages, Little Ice Age famines and epidemics led to peasant revolts. Rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing in 1644; the last emperor hanged himself, and the Manchus swept in as the Qing.
legacy: The Forbidden City, the Great Wall in its famous form, porcelain trade with the world and classic novels like Journey to the West.
culture: Porcelain, Ming novels and the Forbidden City.

name: Qing dynasty
life: A population boom to about 400 million farmers.
food: Rice, maize and the Manchu–Han imperial feast.
summary: China's last imperial dynasty.
government: The Manchu Qing ruled with a dual Manchu–Han bureaucracy and the Eight Banners military system. Emperors Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong (1661–1796) presided over a long era of prosperity and territorial expansion into Tibet, Xinjiang and Mongolia.
architecture: The Qing expanded the Summer Palace and Old Summer Palace (destroyed by British and French troops in 1860), and the Potala-style temples at Chengde.
technology: Qing China adopted Jesuit astronomy and cartography, but by the 19th century fell behind Europe's industrial technology.
rise: The Manchus, unified by Nurhaci, took Beijing in 1644 after the Ming collapse.
fall: Population pressure, corruption, the Opium Wars (1839–42, 1856–60), the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) and other revolts, unequal treaties, defeat by Japan (1895), and the Boxer Rebellion (1900) undermined the dynasty. The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule.
legacy: Modern China's borders largely reflect Qing conquests.
culture: Peking opera and Qing literature.

name: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla
life: Farmers and aristocratic elites.
food: Rice, barley and fermented vegetables.
summary: Silla's capital Gyeongju had an observatory (Cheomseongdae).
government: In the Three Kingdoms period, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla were monarchies ruled with powerful aristocracies. Silla used the 'bone-rank' system: birth into 'sacred bone' or 'true bone' lineages decided who could hold office.
architecture: Goguryeo left painted tombs and mountain fortresses. Baekje's Mireuksa temple pagoda and Silla's capital Gyeongju (Cheomseongdae observatory, Bulguksa temple, Seokguram grotto) survive.
technology: Silla's Cheomseongdae (7th century) is among the oldest surviving observatories in East Asia. Baekje transmitted writing, Buddhism and craftsmen to Japan. All three produced superb gold crowns and metalwork.
rise: The kingdoms took shape from the 1st century BCE to the 4th century CE. Goguryeo grew to rule much of Manchuria under Gwanggaeto the Great (r. 391–413).
fall: Silla allied with Tang China to conquer Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668), then expelled the Tang by 676 to unify most of the peninsula. Unified Silla later split amid noble revolts and gave way to Goryeo in 935.
legacy: The first unification of Korea, Korean Buddhist art and the transmission of continental culture to Japan.
culture: Buddhist temples such as Bulguksa.

name: Joseon Korea
life: Confucian society of yangban, farmers and artisans.
food: Rice, kimchi (chilli was added in the 18th century) and many banchan side dishes.
summary: King Sejong created Hangul.
government: Joseon was a Neo-Confucian monarchy run by scholar-officials (yangban) chosen by civil service examinations. Royal records (the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty) were kept with such independence that even kings could not read them.
architecture: Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces in Seoul, Jongmyo royal shrine and the Hwaseong fortress at Suwon.
technology: King Sejong (r. 1418–1450) commissioned Hangul (1443), a phonetic alphabet designed so ordinary people could read. His scholars also built rain gauges, water clocks and sundials. Admiral Yi Sun-sin's ironclad 'turtle ships' defeated Japanese fleets in the 1590s.
rise: General Yi Seong-gye overthrew the Goryeo dynasty in 1392 and moved the capital to Hanyang (Seoul).
fall: Japanese (1592–98) and Manchu (1627, 1636) invasions devastated the country. Factional strife and isolation as the 'Hermit Kingdom' followed. Japan forced open its ports (1876), made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910.
legacy: Hangul, Confucian family culture and one of the world's longest-ruling dynasties (518 years).
culture: Hangul, pansori and kimchi culture.

name: Heian Japan
known_for: The Tale of Genji, court culture
life: Aristocrats in Kyoto; peasants farmed rice.
food: Rice, fish and vegetables; Buddhism discouraged meat.
summary: The world's first novel by Murasaki Shikibu.
government: The emperor reigned in Heian-kyō (Kyoto), but real power passed to the Fujiwara clan, who ruled as regents by marrying daughters into the imperial family. Later, retired emperors ruled 'from the cloister' (insei).
architecture: Kyoto was laid out on a grid modelled on Chang'an. Byōdō-in's Phoenix Hall and shinden-style aristocratic mansions with gardens and ponds also survive.
technology: The kana syllabaries developed, letting writers, many of them court women, write Japanese phonetically.
rise: Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō in 794 to escape the power of Nara's Buddhist monasteries.
fall: Provincial warrior clans grew strong. The Genpei War (1180–85) between the Taira and Minamoto ended with Minamoto no Yoritomo founding the Kamakura shogunate in 1185.
legacy: Murasaki Shikibu's The Tale of Genji (~1010), often called the world's first novel, and Sei Shōnagon's Pillow Book.
culture: The Tale of Genji and waka poetry.

name: Edo Japan (Tokugawa)
life: Samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants.
food: Rice, miso, tofu; sushi and tempura stalls in Edo.
summary: Edo became one of the largest cities.
government: The shogun ruled from Edo, while about 260 daimyo governed their domains. The 'alternate attendance' system (sankin-kōtai) made daimyo spend every other year in Edo and leave families there as hostages. Society was ranked as samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants.
architecture: Edo Castle, Himeji Castle (completed 1609), Nikkō's Tōshō-gū shrine and merchant townhouses.
technology: Japan was largely closed to foreigners (sakoku) except the Dutch at Dejima, through whom 'Dutch learning' (rangaku) brought European medicine and science. Literacy was high and woodblock printing (ukiyo-e) became a mass art.
rise: Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara (1600) and became shogun in 1603, ending a century of civil war.
fall: Commodore Perry's US ships (1853) forced Japan open. Unequal treaties and domestic unrest followed, and samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the shogunate in the Meiji Restoration (1868).
legacy: Two and a half centuries of peace, haiku (Bashō), kabuki, Hokusai's woodblock prints and the foundations of modern Japan.
culture: Kabuki, haiku (Bashō) and ukiyo-e prints.

name: Funan
life: Farmers and port traders.
food: Rice from the Mekong delta and fish.
summary: An early Southeast Asian state.
government: Funan, known from Chinese records, was ruled by kings, said to descend from the marriage of an Indian Brahmin named Kaundinya and a local queen named Soma.
architecture: Óc Eo, its port in the Mekong delta, had canals linking it to inland cities, brick buildings and workshops.
technology: Canals for drainage and transport. Roman, Indian and Chinese goods have been found at Óc Eo.
rise: It grew from about the 1st century CE as a stop on the sea route between India and China.
fall: Shifts in shipping routes through the Strait of Malacca weakened it, and by the 7th century Chenla had absorbed it.
legacy: The earliest Indianised state of mainland Southeast Asia.
culture: Hindu and Buddhist worship.

name: Srivijaya
life: Sailors and traders around Palembang.
food: Rice, sago, fish and spices.
summary: Studied by Chinese pilgrim Yijing.
government: A thalassocracy: maharajas at Palembang controlled the Strait of Malacca and Sunda Strait through allied ports and the loyalty of sea peoples (orang laut).
architecture: Little survives at Palembang. Related monuments include Muara Takus and, in Java, the Sailendra dynasty's Borobudur.
technology: Navigation with monsoon winds and control of shipping and taxes on the China–India sea trade.
rise: Srivijaya emerged around 650 CE in Sumatra. The Chinese monk Yijing (671) found over a thousand monks studying there.
fall: The Chola king Rajendra I raided its ports in 1025. Later, Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit took over its role.
legacy: A major centre of Buddhist learning; Old Malay inscriptions are the ancestors of Malay and Indonesian.
culture: Buddhist learning centres.

name: Khmer Empire
life: Rice farmers supporting temple cities.
food: Rice, fish (prahok paste) and fruit.
summary: Angkor may have been the largest pre-industrial city.
government: The god-king (devaraja) cult linked the Khmer king to Shiva or Vishnu. The king ruled a vast network of provinces through officials and temple foundations.
architecture: Angkor Wat (early 12th century, built by Suryavarman II) is the largest religious monument in the world. Angkor Thom, the faces of the Bayon, and Ta Prohm (built by Jayavarman VII) also survive.
technology: A huge hydraulic system of barays (reservoirs), canals and moats. Lidar shows Angkor was a sprawling low-density city of perhaps 750,000–900,000 people.
rise: Jayavarman II declared independence from Java and himself universal monarch in 802 at Phnom Kulen.
fall: Overstretched water infrastructure, alternating mega-droughts and floods in the 14th–15th centuries, a shift to Theravada Buddhism and maritime trade, and attacks by Ayutthaya (1431) led the capital to move south.
legacy: Angkor Wat is on Cambodia's flag. Khmer architecture influenced all of mainland Southeast Asia.
culture: Apsara dance and Angkor's reliefs.

name: Majapahit
life: Farmers and traders across Java.
food: Rice, spices and coconut.
summary: Inspired Indonesian nationalism.
government: Kings ruled from Trowulan in East Java with powerful ministers, most famously Gajah Mada, who swore the Palapa oath not to rest until the archipelago was united.
architecture: Red-brick temples (candi) and gates such as Bajang Ratu, with the canals of Trowulan.
technology: Rice irrigation, a large fleet and the spice trade.
rise: Raden Wijaya used a Mongol invasion force to defeat his rival in 1293, then drove the Mongols out.
fall: Succession wars, the rise of Muslim port states such as Demak and Malacca, and Demak's conquest around 1527.
legacy: A symbol of Indonesian unity; the Nagarakretagama poem. Bali preserves its Hindu culture.
culture: Wayang shadow puppetry and Old Javanese poetry.

name: Polynesian voyagers
known_for: Wayfinding by stars, swells and birds
life: Settled Hawaii, New Zealand, Easter Island
food: Voyagers carried 'canoe plants' — taro, breadfruit, yam, banana, sugarcane, coconut and later sweet potato — plus pigs, dogs and chickens. Fish and shellfish provided protein.
summary: Spread across the largest area of any pre-modern culture.
government: Chiefs (ariki) of ranked lineages, tracing descent from gods and founding canoe voyagers, led island societies. Hawai'i and Tonga developed paramount kingships.
architecture: Marae temples, Tonga's Ha'amonga trilithon, Rapa Nui's moai statues and Hawai'i's heiau and fishponds.
technology: Double-hulled voyaging canoes navigated without instruments, using star paths, ocean swells, birds and clouds. The Hōkūleʻa voyages since 1976 proved such journeys possible.
rise: Lapita ancestors reached Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BCE. Their descendants settled East Polynesia, Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa (~1250 CE).
fall: European contact from the 18th century brought diseases that killed many, missionaries, plantations and colonial annexation.
legacy: The most widespread human migration before modern times, across a third of the globe's surface.
culture: Tattooing, navigation lore and oral genealogies.

name: Minoan civilisation
life: People farmed olives, grapes and grain, raised sheep for wool, fished, and worked as potters and metalworkers. Women appear prominently in religious scenes.
food: Olives, wine, honey, barley, legumes and fish; storage jars (pithoi) filled palace magazines.
summary: Weakened by the Thera eruption.
government: Minoan Crete was organised around large 'palaces' at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, which acted as administrative, religious and storage centres, collecting and redistributing oil, wine and grain recorded in Linear A. Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, Minoan art shows no images of a mighty warrior-king, and towns lacked strong walls, suggesting a relatively peaceful society under priestly or elite rule, perhaps with prominent priestesses.
architecture: Knossos covered about 20,000 m² with multi-storey wings around a central court, columns tapering downward, light wells, grand staircases, and painted frescoes of dolphins, bull-leaping and processions. It had clay pipes for water and drainage, and some of the earliest flushing toilets. Its maze-like plan may have inspired the labyrinth myth.
technology: Minoans were skilled sailors who traded across the Aegean, Egypt and the Levant. They made fine pottery like Kamares ware, gold jewellery and seal stones, and wrote Linear A (undeciphered) and Cretan hieroglyphs. The Phaistos Disc is the earliest stamped text.
rise: Neolithic farmers settled Crete around 7000 BCE. By about 2000 BCE wealth from olive oil, wine and sea trade allowed palaces to rise. After an earthquake destroyed them around 1700 BCE, even grander 'new palaces' were built.
fall: The eruption of Thera around 1600 BCE devastated Minoan towns and trade. Around 1450 BCE most palaces were burned, and Mycenaean Greeks took over Knossos, writing in Linear B. Minoan culture faded by about 1100 BCE.
legacy: Arthur Evans named the civilisation after the mythical King Minos when he excavated Knossos (from 1900). Minoan art and myths of the Minotaur, Daedalus and Icarus shaped European imagination.
culture: Religion centred on goddesses, sacred horns, the double axe (labrys) and peak sanctuaries; bull-leaping was a ritual sport.

name: Mycenaean Greece
life: Most people farmed, raised livestock and worked for palaces as craftsmen or labourers.
food: Barley, wheat, olive oil, figs and wine; Linear B tablets record rations.
summary: Fell in the Bronze Age collapse.
government: Mycenaean Greece was a set of palace kingdoms — Mycenae, Pylos, Tiryns, Thebes — each ruled by a wanax (king) with officials like the lawagetas (military leader). Linear B tablets from Pylos record taxes, rations, land holdings, bronze smiths and slaves, showing a centralised palace economy.
architecture: Massive 'Cyclopean' walls made of huge stones (Greeks later thought giants built them), the Lion Gate of Mycenae (about 1250 BCE), megaron throne halls and beehive tholos tombs like the Treasury of Atreus.
technology: Bronze weapons and armour, chariots, and Linear B — the earliest form of Greek, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952. Their ships traded across the Mediterranean.
rise: Mainland Greek chiefdoms grew rich from about 1650 BCE, as shown by the gold death masks of Mycenae's Shaft Graves (including the 'Mask of Agamemnon'). They absorbed Minoan culture and took over Crete around 1450 BCE.
fall: Around 1200 BCE palaces were burned and abandoned in the Bronze Age collapse. Causes included drought, earthquakes, internal revolts and attacks; Greece entered a 'Dark Age' without writing.
legacy: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey preserve memories of the Mycenaean world; heroes like Agamemnon, Achilles and Odysseus are set in it.
culture: They worshipped gods like Zeus, Poseidon and Dionysus, recorded in Linear B.

name: Classical Greece
life: Citizens farmed, traded and served as soldiers; women managed households with limited rights in Athens but more in Sparta; slaves did much labour.
food: Bread or barley porridge, olives, cheese, figs and wine mixed with water; meat came mainly from sacrifices. Spartans ate a notorious black broth.
summary: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Parthenon.
government: Hundreds of city-states (poleis) had different constitutions. Athens built a direct democracy in which citizen men voted in the Assembly and juries were chosen by lot after Cleisthenes' reforms (508 BCE). Sparta was a militarised oligarchy with two kings.
architecture: Greek architects developed the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders. The Parthenon (447–432 BCE) used subtle curves to look perfectly straight; theatres like Epidaurus had remarkable acoustics; and cities had an agora, stoas, temples and gymnasia.
technology: Greeks developed the trireme warship, advances in geometry (Pythagoras, Euclid), astronomy (Aristarchus proposed a Sun-centred model), medicine (Hippocrates) and engineering, including the Antikythera mechanism, an analogue astronomical computer from the Hellenistic period.
rise: After the Greek Dark Ages, city-states revived from the 8th century BCE with the alphabet, colonies and the Olympic Games (776 BCE). They defeated Persia at Marathon (490), Salamis (480) and Plataea (479).
fall: The Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) exhausted Athens and Sparta. Thebes briefly dominated, then Philip II of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea (338 BCE). Rome conquered Greece in 146 BCE.
legacy: Democracy, philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle), drama (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Aristophanes), history (Herodotus, Thucydides), the Olympic Games, mathematics and science all shaped Western and world civilisation.
culture: Greeks worshipped the Olympian gods and held festivals like the Panathenaia and Dionysia, with theatre.

name: Macedonian Empire
life: Soldiers settled in new cities; Greek became the common language of trade.
food: Greek foods spread across the east; Alexander's troops encountered sugarcane ('honey without bees') in India.
summary: Reached the Beas River in Punjab (326 BCE).
government: Philip II reformed Macedon into a powerful monarchy and dominated Greece through the League of Corinth. Alexander ruled as king of Macedon, hegemon of Greece, pharaoh of Egypt and Great King of Persia, keeping Persian satrapies and officials, and encouraging intermarriage between Macedonians and Persians (the Susa weddings, 324 BCE).
architecture: Alexander founded around 20 cities named Alexandria, including Alexandria in Egypt with its Lighthouse (Pharos) and Library. The royal tombs at Vergina, including Philip II's, contain painted frescoes and gold.
technology: The Macedonian phalanx with 6-metre sarissa pikes, combined with Companion cavalry, plus siege engineers who built towers and torsion catapults, made Alexander's army formidable.
rise: Philip II (r. 359–336 BCE) built a professional army and defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea (338). Alexander, after Philip's assassination, conquered Persia, Egypt and lands to the Indus in 334–325 BCE.
fall: Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32, without a clear heir. His generals (the Diadochi) fought the Wars of the Successors, splitting the empire into the Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid kingdoms; Rome conquered Macedon in 168 BCE.
legacy: The Hellenistic age spread Greek language, art and science from Egypt to Afghanistan and influenced Indian art in Gandhara.
culture: Greek gods and culture mixed with Egyptian, Persian and Indian traditions.

name: Roman Republic
life: Most Romans were farmers or urban workers; patron-client relationships tied rich and poor.
food: Puls (wheat porridge), bread, olives, cheese and vegetables; garum fish sauce.
summary: Conquered the Mediterranean; ended with Julius Caesar and Augustus.
government: The Roman Republic (509–27 BCE) balanced power among two consuls elected annually, a Senate of former magistrates that controlled finances and foreign policy, and popular assemblies that elected officials and passed laws. Tribunes of the plebs could veto actions harmful to commoners. In emergencies, a dictator could be appointed for six months. The Twelve Tables (451–450 BCE) were Rome's first written laws.
architecture: The Republic built the Via Appia (312 BCE), aqueducts like the Aqua Appia, basilicas and temples in the Forum, and invented Roman concrete with volcanic ash (pozzolana), allowing arches and vaults.
technology: Roman engineers built roads, bridges and aqueducts; the legion's organisation, training and equipment (the gladius and pilum) made it highly effective.
rise: After expelling King Tarquin the Proud in 509 BCE, Rome conquered its Latin, Etruscan and Samnite neighbours, defeated Pyrrhus and Carthage (Punic Wars), and took Greece, Spain and the eastern Mediterranean.
fall: Conquest brought wealth to the elite while small farmers lost land. The Gracchi brothers' reforms ended in their murders; Marius's army reforms created soldiers loyal to generals; civil wars between Marius and Sulla, then Caesar and Pompey, followed. After Caesar's assassination, Octavian became Augustus in 27 BCE.
legacy: The Republic inspired the US Constitution and later democracies: the Senate, checks and balances, vetoes and the idea of citizenship.
culture: Romans honoured ancestors and gods like Jupiter, and valued virtue (virtus) and duty (pietas).

name: Roman Empire
known_for: Roads, aqueducts, concrete, Roman law, Christianity
life: City dwellers in insulae, peasants and enslaved workers.
food: Bread was so central that the state distributed free grain (the annona) to about 200,000 Roman citizens; Egyptian grain fleets fed the capital. Wealthy Romans dined reclining on dormice, oysters and peacock, recorded in Apicius' cookbook.
summary: The Western Empire fell in 476 CE; the Eastern lasted to 1453.
government: Augustus kept the outward forms of the Republic (Senate, consuls) but held real power as princeps, 'first citizen', commanding the army and controlling key provinces. The empire was divided into provinces governed by senators or imperial appointees. Roman law developed into a sophisticated system, and citizenship expanded until in 212 CE the emperor Caracalla granted it to nearly all free inhabitants. Society divided into senators, equestrians, citizens, freedmen and enslaved people.
architecture: Romans perfected the arch, vault and dome using concrete: the Pantheon (~125 CE) still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome. They built the Colosseum (seating ~50,000), aqueducts like the Pont du Gard, baths, basilicas, triumphal arches, theatres, apartment blocks (insulae) and planned colonial towns with grid streets, forums and sewers like the Cloaca Maxima.
technology: Roman engineers built over 80,000 km of paved roads, aqueducts carrying water by gravity over long distances, hydraulic mining, water mills, cranes powered by treadwheels, underfloor heating (hypocausts), glass-blowing, and concrete using volcanic ash that self-heals in seawater. Medicine advanced under Galen, and the Julian calendar (46 BCE) was a lasting reform.
rise: Rome grew from a city-state to master of Italy and then the Mediterranean through disciplined citizen legions, alliances, colonies and road-building. After a century of civil wars ended with Octavian's victory at Actium (31 BCE), the Senate granted him the title Augustus (27 BCE), beginning the Empire. Expansion continued until Trajan's reign (117 CE).
fall: The Western Empire weakened over centuries: the Crisis of the Third Century (235–284) brought civil wars, plague, invasions and inflation; Diocletian divided the empire; and it was formally split in 395. Pressure from Germanic peoples displaced by the Huns, the Visigoths' sack of Rome (410), the Vandals' seizure of North Africa's grain (439) and their sack of Rome (455) left the West unable to pay its armies. In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus. The Eastern Empire continued until 1453.
legacy: Roman law underlies many legal systems; Latin gave rise to the Romance languages and much scientific vocabulary; Christianity spread through the empire; and Roman architecture, engineering, the calendar and ideas of citizenship shaped Europe and beyond.
culture: Baths, games, Latin literature.

name: Byzantine Empire
known_for: Hagia Sophia, Justinian's code, Orthodox Christianity
life: Constantinople had perhaps 500,000 people; chariot races in the Hippodrome drew fans of Blue and Green factions.
food: Bread, fish, olive oil, cheese, wine and fasting foods for Orthodox fasts.
summary: Fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
government: The Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire was ruled by an emperor seen as God's representative, crowned by the Patriarch of Constantinople. A large salaried bureaucracy, the theme system of military provinces and a professional army supported him. Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis codified Roman law. Palace intrigue, blinding of rivals and coups were common.
architecture: Hagia Sophia (537), whose dome seemed to float, was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years. The Theodosian Walls protected Constantinople for a millennium. Byzantine mosaics decorate Ravenna and Kyiv.
technology: Greek fire, a liquid weapon that burned on water, destroyed Arab fleets. The gold solidus coin was stable for 700 years, and Constantinople's silk industry used smuggled silkworms.
rise: Constantine founded Constantinople (330) on the site of Byzantium. When the Western Empire fell in 476, the East continued. Justinian (r. 527–565) reconquered Italy and North Africa.
fall: Arab conquests took Egypt and Syria in the 7th century; Seljuks won at Manzikert (1071); the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople (1204). The Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453.
legacy: Byzantium preserved Greek classics, spread Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic alphabet to the Slavs, and its scholars helped spark the Renaissance.
culture: Orthodox Christianity, icons and theological debates, including the Iconoclasm controversy.

name: Celts
known_for: Hill forts, La Tène art, druids
life: People farmed, raised cattle and lived in roundhouses; feasting and raiding were central.
food: Wheat, barley, pork, beer and mead.
summary: Conquered by Rome except in Ireland and northern Britain.
government: Celtic peoples were organised into tribes led by kings or chiefs and warrior aristocracies. Druids served as priests, judges, teachers and keepers of oral law and lore; they trained for up to 20 years. Women sometimes led, like Boudica of the Iceni.
architecture: Celts built hillforts such as Maiden Castle, fortified towns (oppida) like Bibracte and Manching, crannogs (lake dwellings), and roundhouses.
technology: Celts were expert ironworkers, inventing chain mail and making fine swords, shields and torcs in the curvilinear La Tène style.
rise: The Hallstatt culture (about 800–450 BCE) in Austria grew rich from salt mining; La Tène culture (from about 450 BCE) spread across Europe. Celts sacked Rome around 390 BCE and Delphi (279 BCE), and settled Anatolia as the Galatians.
fall: Rome conquered northern Italy, Spain, Gaul (Caesar) and Britain. Germanic migrations later pushed Celtic speakers to the fringes.
legacy: Celtic languages survive in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Brittany; Celtic art inspired the Book of Kells.
culture: They worshipped many gods, held sacred groves, and celebrated Samhain (ancestor of Halloween).

name: Vikings
life: Most Vikings were farmers, fishers and traders; raiding was seasonal.
food: Porridge, bread, dried fish, meat and dairy; ale and mead.
summary: Reached North America ~1000 CE.
government: Viking Age Scandinavia had kings, jarls (earls) and free men (karls), with thralls (slaves) at the bottom. Free men met at the thing assembly to settle disputes and make laws; Iceland's Althing (930) is one of the oldest parliaments.
architecture: Longhouses, ring fortresses like Trelleborg, and later stave churches.
technology: Clinker-built longships with shallow drafts could cross oceans and sail up rivers; sun compasses may have aided navigation. They wrote in runes.
rise: Population pressure, wealth from trade and fast ships led Scandinavians to raid Lindisfarne (793). They settled England's Danelaw, Ireland (Dublin), Normandy, Iceland and Greenland, reached North America (about 1000), and as the Rus founded states in Russia.
fall: Christianisation, stronger kingdoms and the defeat at Stamford Bridge (1066) ended the Viking Age.
legacy: Normandy, Kievan Rus, Iceland's sagas, and words like 'sky', 'egg' and 'window' in English.
culture: They worshipped Odin, Thor and Freyja; skaldic poetry praised heroes.

name: Holy Roman Empire
life: Peasants worked lords' land; towns like Nuremberg and the Hanseatic League's Lübeck flourished through trade.
food: Bread, beer, cabbage and pork.
summary: 'Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire' — Voltaire.
government: The Holy Roman Empire was a loose union of hundreds of kingdoms, duchies, bishoprics and free cities in central Europe. The emperor was elected by prince-electors (seven under the Golden Bull of 1356) and crowned by the pope until 1530. The Imperial Diet (Reichstag) and courts brought rulers together, but real power lay with the princes. From 1438 the emperors were almost always Habsburgs.
architecture: Romanesque cathedrals at Speyer, Worms and Mainz, Charlemagne's Palatine Chapel at Aachen where kings were crowned, and Gothic masterpieces like Cologne Cathedral.
technology: Gutenberg's printing press at Mainz (around 1450) spread knowledge; mining in Saxony and Bohemia (silver of Joachimsthal gave us the word 'dollar') and clockmaking flourished.
rise: Otto I of Saxony defeated the Magyars at Lechfeld (955) and was crowned emperor by the pope in 962, reviving Charlemagne's title.
fall: The Investiture Controversy, the Reformation and the devastating Thirty Years' War (1618–48) weakened imperial authority; the Peace of Westphalia gave princes near-sovereignty. Napoleon defeated Austria and forced Francis II to dissolve the empire in 1806.
legacy: German federalism, as Voltaire mocked: 'neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire'.
culture: Catholic and, after Luther, Protestant Christianity defined the empire's cultural map.

name: Kievan Rus'
life: Most people farmed rye and wheat in forests; cities hosted merchants and craftsmen.
food: Rye bread, kasha and kvass.
summary: Destroyed by the Mongols.
government: Kievan Rus was a federation of East Slavic principalities ruled by the Rurikid dynasty, with the Grand Prince of Kiev at the top. Princes ruled cities with their retinues (druzhina) and councils of boyars; town assemblies (veche) were powerful, especially in Novgorod. Yaroslav the Wise issued the Russkaya Pravda law code.
architecture: St Sophia's Cathedral in Kyiv (1037), with Byzantine mosaics, the Golden Gate, and wooden churches and fortresses.
technology: Rus traders sailed the Dnieper 'route from the Varangians to the Greeks', trading furs, honey, wax and slaves for Byzantine silks and silver.
rise: Varangian (Viking) chiefs led by Rurik and Oleg took control of Novgorod and Kiev in the late 9th century. Vladimir the Great's baptism (988) brought Orthodox Christianity.
fall: Succession disputes split the realm, and the Mongols destroyed Kiev in 1240, ending its unity.
legacy: Christianisation by Vladimir (988); shared heritage of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.
culture: Orthodox Christianity, icons and Old Church Slavonic in Cyrillic script.

name: Spanish Empire
known_for: Conquest of the Americas, silver of Potosí
life: Indigenous people worked in mines and haciendas under forced labour (mita); enslaved Africans worked on plantations; Spanish-born elites held power.
food: The Columbian Exchange brought maize, potatoes, tomatoes and chocolate to Europe and wheat and cattle to the Americas.
summary: 'The empire on which the sun never sets' (first).
government: The Spanish monarchy governed its American empire through the Council of the Indies in Spain and viceroys in Mexico City (New Spain) and Lima (Peru), later also Bogotá and Buenos Aires. Audiencias served as courts, and the encomienda system gave conquistadors the labour of Indigenous people in return for 'protection' and Christian instruction. A rigid caste system ranked people by birth and ancestry.
architecture: Spanish colonial cities were laid out on grids around a central plaza with a cathedral and government palace, following the Laws of the Indies (1573). Baroque churches, such as Mexico City's Metropolitan Cathedral built over the Aztec Templo Mayor, and missions across California and South America remain.
technology: Spanish ships, cannon, steel and horses gave conquistadors advantages, while galleons carried silver across the Atlantic and Pacific (Manila galleons from 1565). Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas, refined with mercury amalgamation, flooded the world economy, much of it ending up in China.
rise: After completing the Reconquista (1492), Spain sponsored Columbus, then conquered the Aztecs (1521) and Incas (1532) with Indigenous allies and the devastation of smallpox. Under Charles V and Philip II, Spain combined American silver with Habsburg possessions in Europe, becoming the dominant world power in the 16th century.
fall: Costly wars, inflation from silver, the expulsion of Jews and Moriscos, and the defeat of the Armada weakened Spain. Napoleon's invasion of Spain (1808) triggered independence wars led by Bolívar, San Martín and Hidalgo, and most of Latin America was free by 1825. Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines to the US in 1898.
legacy: Spanish is the world's second-most spoken native language; Catholicism, legal systems and mixed (mestizo) societies shaped Latin America. The conquest also caused the deaths of millions of Indigenous people and the African slave trade to the Americas.
culture: Catholic missions converted millions, often blending with Indigenous beliefs, as with the Virgin of Guadalupe.

name: Portuguese Empire
life: Settlers, sailors, missionaries and enslaved Africans moved across the empire; Brazil's sugar economy relied on slavery.
food: Spice trade; chillies brought from America to India.
summary: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498.
government: Portugal's empire was a network of fortified trading posts (feitorias) and colonies, governed through viceroys in Goa (the Estado da Índia) and captaincies in Brazil. The crown controlled the spice trade through the Casa da Índia. The cartaz pass system forced Asian ships to buy Portuguese permits.
architecture: Portuguese forts at Elmina (Ghana), Mombasa (Fort Jesus), Diu, Malacca and Macau, and Goa's Basilica of Bom Jesus with St Francis Xavier's tomb, remain. The Manueline style decorated Lisbon's Jerónimos Monastery with maritime motifs.
technology: Portuguese navigators developed the caravel, which could sail against the wind, and used the astrolabe and quadrant to calculate latitude, building on Prince Henry's patronage. Mapmakers charted Africa's coast.
rise: Under Prince Henry the Navigator, Portugal explored Africa's coast; Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape (1488) and Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (1498). Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515), and Cabral claimed Brazil (1500).
fall: The Dutch and English took most Asian posts in the 17th century; Brazil became independent in 1822. Portugal clung to Africa until the Carnation Revolution of 1974 led to independence for Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau. India took Goa in 1961, and Macau returned to China in 1999.
legacy: Portuguese is spoken by about 260 million people. Portugal brought chillies, cashews, potatoes and papaya to India, and words like 'pão' (pav) and 'janela'.
culture: Catholic missions spread across Asia; Goan culture blends Portuguese and Konkani traditions.

name: British Empire
known_for: At its peak ruled ~a quarter of the world's land and people
life: In Britain, imperial trade brought tea, sugar, cotton and wealth, especially to the middle and upper classes. In colonies, life ranged from settler farms to plantations worked by indentured labourers and Indian villages paying heavy revenue.
food: Tea, sugar and spices were traded; slave plantations produced sugar.
summary: India was its most valuable colony.
government: The British Empire was a patchwork: self-governing dominions (Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa) had their own parliaments; crown colonies were ruled by governors; India was ruled first by the East India Company and from 1858 by a Viceroy; and protectorates and princely states were governed indirectly through local rulers. Policy was set in London by Parliament and the Colonial and India Offices. Colonised peoples had little or no representation.
architecture: Britain built government houses, railway stations and churches in neoclassical, Gothic Revival and Indo-Saracenic styles, such as Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, Kolkata's Victoria Memorial and Lutyens's New Delhi. Cantonments and hill stations like Shimla separated Europeans from local populations.
technology: Britain's Industrial Revolution gave it steamships, railways, the telegraph (an undersea cable reached India in 1870) and the Maxim gun. These let it move troops and goods across the world. Surveys mapped colonies, and botanical gardens like Kew transferred crops — tea to India, rubber to Malaya.
rise: England founded colonies in North America and the Caribbean in the 17th century, built on sugar and the Atlantic slave trade. After the Seven Years' War (1756–63) and Plassey (1757) it dominated North America and India. Despite losing the 13 colonies in 1783, it expanded across India, Australia, Africa and Asia. At its height in 1920 it ruled about a quarter of the world's land and people — 'the empire on which the sun never set'.
fall: Two world wars bankrupted Britain, and nationalist movements, above all in India, made empire impossible to sustain. India and Pakistan became independent in 1947; Burma and Ceylon in 1948; the Suez Crisis (1956) showed Britain could no longer act alone; and most African and Caribbean colonies became independent in the 1950s–60s. The handover of Hong Kong to China in 1997 is often seen as its end.
legacy: English became a global language, and parliamentary government, common law, railways and cricket spread through former colonies, many now in the Commonwealth. The empire's legacies also include famines, partitions (India, Ireland, Palestine), arbitrary borders, the slave trade and the drain of wealth from colonies, which historians continue to debate.
culture: British imperial culture promoted a sense of racial and civilisational superiority, while colonised societies blended and resisted it, producing new literatures in English and movements of cultural revival.

name: Russian Empire
known_for: Peter the Great, serfdom, expansion to the Pacific
life: Most people were peasants living in village communes (mir), paying taxes and serving long military terms.
food: Rye bread, cabbage soup (shchi) and kasha.
summary: Ended in the 1917 revolution.
government: The Russian Empire was an autocracy: the tsar held unlimited power, supported by the nobility and the Orthodox Church, with a large bureaucracy and secret police. Peter the Great created a Senate and Table of Ranks. Serfdom bound most peasants to the land until Alexander II freed 23 million serfs in 1861. After the 1905 revolution an elected Duma was created but had limited power.
architecture: Peter the Great built St Petersburg from 1703 on the Neva marshes as a European-style capital, with the Winter Palace and Peterhof designed by architects like Rastrelli. Onion-domed Orthodox churches such as St Basil's Cathedral in Moscow (from Ivan IV's era) are iconic.
technology: Russia built the Trans-Siberian Railway (1891–1916), the longest in the world. Dmitri Mendeleev created the periodic table (1869), and Alexander Popov experimented with radio.
rise: Muscovy threw off Mongol rule under Ivan III and was proclaimed a tsardom by Ivan IV (1547). After the Time of Troubles, the Romanovs (from 1613) expanded across Siberia to the Pacific. Peter the Great defeated Sweden and declared the Russian Empire in 1721; Catherine the Great took Crimea and parts of Poland. It became the largest country on Earth.
fall: Defeat by Japan (1905), revolution, the strain of World War I and food shortages led to the February Revolution of 1917, when Nicholas II abdicated. The Bolsheviks seized power in October, and the royal family was executed in 1918.
legacy: The empire left a vast multi-ethnic territory, and a cultural golden age: Pushkin, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Chekhov and Tchaikovsky.
culture: Orthodox Christianity, icons and church music shaped Russian culture.

name: Soviet Union
life: Soviet citizens had guaranteed jobs, free education and health care, and subsidised housing, but faced shortages, queues and limited freedom. Women entered the workforce in large numbers.
food: Bread, potatoes and cabbage; famines in 1932–33 killed millions.
summary: Dissolved into 15 states in 1991.
government: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) was a one-party state ruled by the Communist Party, nominally a federation of 15 republics. Real power lay with the Party's Politburo and General Secretary. Under Stalin, the secret police (NKVD, later KGB) arrested millions, and the Gulag labour camp system held about 18 million people over its history. The economy was centrally planned through five-year plans.
architecture: Early Soviet architects explored Constructivism; Stalin preferred monumental 'Stalinist Empire' style, such as Moscow's 'Seven Sisters' skyscrapers and ornate metro stations. From the 1950s, millions of prefabricated apartment blocks (khrushchyovkas) were built to address housing shortages.
technology: Rapid industrialisation built steel, dams and tractors. The USSR tested an atomic bomb in 1949, launched Sputnik (1957), the first satellite, and sent Yuri Gagarin into orbit (1961) and Valentina Tereshkova (1963), the first woman. It was a world leader in rocketry, mathematics and chess.
rise: The Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power in the October Revolution of 1917 and won the Russian Civil War (1918–21). The USSR was formed in 1922. Stalin's forced collectivisation and industrialisation transformed the economy at the cost of famines, including the Holodomor in Ukraine. Victory over Nazi Germany in 1945, at the cost of about 27 million lives, made it a superpower controlling Eastern Europe.
fall: Economic stagnation under Brezhnev, the costly war in Afghanistan (1979–89), and the Chernobyl disaster weakened the system. Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms — glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring) — let nationalism and criticism surface. Eastern European communist regimes fell in 1989, a hard-line coup failed in August 1991, and on 26 December 1991 the USSR dissolved into 15 states.
legacy: The USSR defeated Nazism, achieved mass literacy and launched the space age, but its terror, famines and the Gulag killed millions. The Cold War rivalry shaped the second half of the 20th century, and the USSR was a close partner of India from the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty.
culture: Socialist realism dictated art; writers such as Pasternak and Solzhenitsyn faced persecution. The state promoted atheism.

name: Norte Chico (Caral)
known_for: The oldest civilisation in the Americas
life: Fishing villages traded dried fish for cotton nets and vegetables; people lived in small houses around ceremonial centres.
food: Anchovies and sardines from the coast traded for squash, beans and cotton.
summary: Contemporaneous with Egypt's pyramids.
government: Norte Chico (or Caral-Supe) society on Peru's central coast had no evidence of warfare, defensive walls or weapons. Elites probably organised the labour to build monumental platforms through religious authority and control of trade between fishing villages on the coast and cotton-growing inland towns. About 30 urban centres existed.
architecture: Caral, the largest site, has six stepped platform pyramids up to 18 m high, sunken circular plazas and residential areas, built around 2600 BCE — contemporary with Egypt's pyramids. Builders used shicra, mesh bags filled with stones, which made structures resistant to earthquakes.
technology: People grew cotton for fishing nets, squash, beans and chillies with irrigation canals. A knotted string found at Caral may be an early quipu. Flutes made of condor and pelican bones show music.
rise: Around 3000 BCE, rich anchovy and sardine fisheries combined with irrigated cotton farming in the Supe, Pativilca and Fortaleza valleys supported the rise of towns.
fall: Around 1800 BCE the region was abandoned, perhaps due to climate shifts, El Niño floods or sand dunes covering fields, as other Andean centres rose.
legacy: The oldest known civilisation in the Americas, laying foundations for Andean traditions such as platform mounds and quipus.
culture: Ceremonies with music and fire rituals were held in sunken plazas.

name: Olmec
life: Farmers grew maize, beans and squash and fished in rivers; artisans carved jade.
food: Maize processed with lime (nixtamalisation), beans and squash.
summary: The 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica.
government: Olmec centres were ruled by powerful chiefs or kings, depicted on colossal stone heads up to 3 m tall and on 'altars' (actually thrones), which show rulers emerging from caves, linking them to the supernatural.
architecture: San Lorenzo (about 1200–900 BCE) was built on an artificial plateau; La Venta (about 900–400 BCE) had a 30-m earthen pyramid, plazas and buried mosaic pavements of serpentine blocks.
technology: The Olmecs made rubber balls for the Mesoamerican ballgame, possibly developed the earliest Mesoamerican writing (the Cascajal Block) and the Long Count calendar, and carved jade and basalt brought from far away.
rise: Around 1500 BCE, farming villages in the fertile river lowlands of Veracruz and Tabasco grew into the first complex society in Mesoamerica.
fall: By 400 BCE Olmec centres were abandoned, possibly due to rivers changing course, volcanic activity, or overuse of land.
legacy: Often called Mesoamerica's 'mother culture', the Olmec influenced the Maya and later peoples in religion, ballgames, calendars and art, such as the feathered serpent and were-jaguar.
culture: They worshipped jaguar-like deities and practised ritual bloodletting.

name: Maya civilisation
known_for: Full writing system, calendar, zero, astronomy
life: Most people were farmers in thatched houses growing maize in milpas; nobles, scribes and artisans lived near city centres.
food: Maize was sacred; people ate tortillas, tamales and atole, with beans, squash, chilli and turkey. Elites drank frothy cacao.
summary: Classic cities declined amid drought and war around 800–900 CE.
government: Maya cities were independent city-states ruled by divine kings (k'uhul ajaw) who performed bloodletting rituals and led wars. Great powers such as Tikal and Calakmul built alliance networks and fought 'star wars' timed by Venus. Kings recorded their deeds on stone stelae.
architecture: Maya cities had stepped pyramids such as Tikal's Temple I, palaces, ball courts, causeways (sacbeob) and observatories like Chichén Itzá's El Caracol. Lidar surveys since 2018 have revealed millions of buildings and huge farming systems around cities.
technology: The Maya developed a full writing system of about 800 glyphs, deciphered mostly since the 1970s; the concept of zero; the Long Count calendar; and accurate astronomical tables in the Dresden Codex. They built reservoirs and raised fields.
rise: Maya villages appeared by 2000 BCE; large Preclassic cities like El Mirador and Nakbé rose by 600 BCE. The Classic period (250–900 CE) saw dozens of great cities.
fall: Classic southern cities were abandoned around 800–950 CE after droughts, warfare and overpopulation. Northern cities and highland kingdoms lasted until Spanish conquest (the last, Nojpetén, fell in 1697).
legacy: About six million Maya live in Mexico, Guatemala and Belize today, speaking about 30 Maya languages and preserving the Popol Vuh and traditions.
culture: Maize gods, the underworld Xibalba, the Hero Twins and the ballgame were central to religion.

name: Teotihuacan
known_for: Pyramids of the Sun and Moon
life: Residents lived in apartment compounds organised by family or trade; neighbourhoods housed migrants from Oaxaca and the Gulf coast.
food: Maize, beans, squash, amaranth and pulque.
summary: Its name means 'place where the gods were created'.
government: Teotihuacan's rulers are mysterious: there are few images of individual kings, leading some scholars to suggest collective or council rule. Its influence reached the Maya; a Teotihuacan warrior, Siyaj K'ak', installed a new king at Tikal in 378 CE.
architecture: The city covered 20 km² on a grid aligned 15.5° east of north, along the 'Avenue of the Dead', with the Pyramid of the Sun (about 65 m), Pyramid of the Moon, and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. About 2,000 multi-family apartment compounds housed residents.
technology: Teotihuacan controlled obsidian mines and workshops making blades, and had standardised architecture with talud-tablero style.
rise: It grew from about 100 BCE, possibly boosted by refugees from the eruption of Popocatépetl and Xitle, reaching 100,000–200,000 people by 450 CE — one of the largest cities in the world.
fall: Around 550 CE the centre was burned, perhaps in an internal revolt amid drought and inequality; the city declined.
legacy: The Aztecs, who found its ruins, named it Teotihuacan, 'the place where gods were born', and believed the current sun was born there.
culture: They worshipped the Feathered Serpent, the Storm God and the Great Goddess.

name: Aztec Empire
life: Commoners (macehualtin) farmed and served in the army; children attended schools.
food: Maize tortillas, beans, squash, chilli, amaranth and chinampa vegetables; nobles drank chocolate.
summary: Tenochtitlan (~200,000) fell to Cortés and smallpox.
government: The Aztec Empire was the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, formed in 1428. The huey tlatoani ('great speaker') was elected by a council of nobles. Conquered city-states kept their own rulers but paid tribute in maize, cotton, cacao, feathers and gold, recorded in the Codex Mendoza.
architecture: Tenochtitlan, on an island in Lake Texcoco, had about 200,000 people, causeways, aqueducts from Chapultepec and the Templo Mayor, a twin pyramid to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc.
technology: Chinampas — floating gardens — produced several harvests a year; dikes separated fresh and salt water.
rise: The Mexica arrived in the Valley of Mexico as poor migrants, founding Tenochtitlan in 1325; under Itzcoatl they overthrew Azcapotzalco, and Moctezuma I and Ahuitzotl expanded the empire.
fall: Spanish conquistadors under Cortés, allied with tens of thousands of Tlaxcalans and others, and aided by smallpox, besieged Tenochtitlan, which fell in 1521.
legacy: Mexico City stands on Tenochtitlan; Nahuatl words like chocolate, tomato and avocado spread worldwide.
culture: Religion required human sacrifice to sustain the sun; poets like Nezahualcoyotl wrote verse.

name: Inca Empire
known_for: Machu Picchu, 40,000 km of roads, quipu knots
life: Communities (ayllu) farmed potatoes and maize collectively and herded llamas.
food: Potatoes (freeze-dried as chuño), maize, quinoa and llama meat; storehouses (qollqa) held food for years.
summary: The largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas.
government: The Sapa Inca, believed to descend from the sun god Inti, ruled Tawantinsuyu through four provinces with governors and a decimal administration. Instead of taxes in money, subjects owed mit'a labour on roads, farms and armies. Conquered peoples were sometimes relocated (mitmaq) to prevent revolt.
architecture: Inca masons fitted huge stones without mortar, as at Sacsayhuamán and Cusco; Machu Picchu (about 1450) was a royal estate. Terraces made mountainsides farmable.
technology: About 40,000 km of roads (Qhapaq Ñan) with rope suspension bridges; relay runners (chasquis); quipus recorded numbers; storehouses (qollqa) held food for years.
rise: Pachacuti (r. 1438–1471) defeated the Chanka and expanded the Cusco kingdom; his son Topa Inca expanded it from Ecuador to Chile.
fall: Smallpox killed Huayna Capac, causing civil war between his sons. Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532; Vilcabamba resisted until 1572.
legacy: About 8 million speak Quechua; the potato spread worldwide.
culture: Inti, the earth mother Pachamama and mummified ancestors were worshipped.

name: Ancestral Puebloans
life: People farmed maize, beans and squash and made pottery.
food: Maize, beans and squash, plus wild game.
summary: Abandoned many sites during the great drought of 1276–99.
government: The Ancestral Puebloans (Anasazi) of the Four Corners region lived in villages led by clan and religious leaders; Chaco Canyon may have been a ceremonial and political centre.
architecture: Great houses like Pueblo Bonito (about 800 rooms) at Chaco Canyon, and cliff dwellings like Mesa Verde's Cliff Palace, built in alcoves.
technology: Water management, roads up to 60 km straight, and astronomical alignments like Fajada Butte's 'sun dagger'.
rise: From about 750 CE farming communities grew maize in the arid southwest; Chaco flourished from 850 to 1150.
fall: Drought (including the Great Drought, 1276–1299) and conflict led people to migrate south and east.
legacy: Descendants include the Hopi, Zuni and Rio Grande Pueblos.
culture: Kivas, underground ceremonial rooms, were central to religion.

name: Mississippian culture
life: Farmers lived in thatched houses around plazas.
food: Maize, beans and squash.
summary: Monks Mound is the largest pre-Columbian earthwork north of Mexico.
government: Mississippian chiefdoms were ruled by paramount chiefs and elites, with Cahokia the largest.
architecture: Cahokia's Monks Mound covers 6 hectares — the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas; 'Woodhenge' circles of posts tracked the sun.
technology: Intensive maize farming and copper and shell crafts.
rise: Cahokia grew rapidly around 1050 CE to perhaps 10,000–20,000 people.
fall: Floods, drought, political instability and deforestation led to Cahokia's abandonment by 1350.
legacy: It was the largest city north of Mexico before the 18th century.
culture: The Southeastern Ceremonial Complex shows birdman imagery.

name: Haudenosaunee Confederacy
life: Women farmed and owned houses; men hunted and fought.
food: The Three Sisters: maize, beans and squash planted together.
summary: Influenced debates about American federalism.
government: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy united the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca (and later Tuscarora) under the Great Law of Peace. A Grand Council of 50 chiefs (hoyaneh) made decisions by consensus; clan mothers chose and could remove them.
architecture: Longhouses up to 100 m long housed several families of a matrilineal clan; villages were palisaded.
technology: The Three Sisters farming (maize, beans, squash) and wampum belts recording treaties.
rise: Tradition says the Peacemaker (Deganawida) and Hiawatha united warring nations; dates range from 1142 to around 1450.
fall: Wars, disease and siding with Britain in the American Revolution led to land loss.
legacy: Some historians argue it influenced the US Constitution; it still exists.
culture: Ceremonies like the Green Corn festival marked the year.

name: United States
life: Americans' lives changed from farming (90% rural in 1790) to industrial cities and then suburbs. Millions of immigrants arrived through Ellis Island; millions of enslaved Africans worked on plantations until 1865. The 20th century brought cars, television and mass consumer culture.
food: Corn, wheat and beef; fast food spread worldwide in the 20th century.
summary: Became the leading world power after 1945.
government: The United States is a federal constitutional republic created by the Constitution of 1787, the oldest written national constitution still in use. Power is divided between the federal government and the states, and federal power is split among Congress (Senate and House), the President, and the courts, led by the Supreme Court, which can strike down laws. The Bill of Rights (1791) protects free speech, religion and fair trials. Voting was first limited to white male property owners; the 15th (1870), 19th (1920) amendments and the Voting Rights Act (1965) extended it to Black citizens and women.
architecture: Early public buildings such as the Capitol and the White House followed neoclassical models, symbolising links to the Roman Republic. Chicago pioneered the steel-framed skyscraper after the 1871 fire, leading to the Empire State Building (1931). Frank Lloyd Wright developed 'organic' architecture, and the interstate highway system (from 1956) reshaped cities into suburbs.
technology: Americans invented or commercialised the cotton gin (1793), telegraph (Morse, 1844), telephone (Bell, 1876), electric light and power grid (Edison), aeroplane (Wright brothers, 1903) and assembly-line car (Ford, 1913). The Manhattan Project built the atomic bomb, NASA landed humans on the Moon (1969), and Silicon Valley developed the microchip, personal computer and internet, built on the Pentagon's ARPANET.
rise: Thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic coast declared independence in 1776 and won it in 1783. The country expanded west through the Louisiana Purchase (1803), war with Mexico (1846–48) and the forced removal of Native Americans (Trail of Tears, 1830s). After the Civil War ended slavery, industrialisation and immigration made the US the world's largest economy by about 1890; victory in the two world wars made it a superpower.
fall: The United States has not fallen. It faced existential crises: the Civil War (1861–65), the Great Depression and the civil rights struggle. Since the Cold War's end it has been the sole superpower, though China's rise, political polarisation and debt are debated as signs of relative decline.
legacy: The US Constitution and Declaration of Independence inspired democratic movements worldwide, while slavery, segregation and the treatment of Native Americans remain painful legacies. American culture — jazz, Hollywood, rock and hip-hop — and companies like Apple and Google shape global life. The US led the creation of the UN, NATO, the World Bank and IMF after 1945.
culture: Christianity, especially Protestant denominations, has shaped American culture, alongside religious freedom. Jazz, blues and rock 'n' roll grew from African American music; Hollywood dominated world cinema.
